# Project overview

## Background

In every EU country women live longer than men. The size of that difference, however, is not the same everywhere. Press coverage of Eurostat figures places the three Baltic states at the top of the list: in 2024 Latvia had the widest gap in the EU, close to ten years, followed by Lithuania and Estonia. These figures are checked against the data in this analysis.

A gap of almost ten years means that many Baltic men do not live to see retirement, while the women around them do. I live in Latvia, so this isn't an abstract statistic for me. It made me want to find out what sits behind it, and whether the Baltic men simply follow a European pattern or fall outside it.

## Aim

The aim of this project is to describe the gap in life expectancy between women and men across the EU, and to identify which country-level factors are associated with it, with the Baltic states as the focus.

## Research question

**Main question:** Why do men in the Baltic states die so much earlier than women, compared with the rest of the EU?

**Sub-questions:**

1.  Which country-level factors (causes of death, alcohol, income, education) are associated with the size of the gap?
2.  How has the gap changed between 2015 and 2024?
3.  Where do Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania sit compared with the other EU countries?

**Scope:**

- **The measure:** life expectancy at birth, women minus men, in years, referred to as "the gap".
- **The countries:** the EU member states, about 27.
- **The period:** 2015 to 2024, or the latest year available in each table.
- **The level:** countries, not individuals. Every number is a national figure.

With about 27 countries, the data can show which factors go together, not what causes what. The analysis therefore uses "is associated with" or "goes with", never "causes".

## Assumptions

**Rationale:** the expected findings are written down before any data is opened. This allows the results to be compared with the initial expectations, and prevents the story from being adjusted to fit the results afterwards.

**Expected message:** Baltic men die earlier, and this goes mainly with heart disease deaths before 65.

**The factor expected to matter most:** deaths from heart and circulatory disease among men under 65. They are the most common cause of early death for men in the Baltics, and many of these men die decades before the women. Accidents and suicide are expected to come second. Alcohol is expected to sit behind both, which is why alcohol-related deaths are included in the data.

**Hypotheses (expectations, not results):**

1.  A bigger gap is associated with more men dying under 65 from heart and circulatory disease.
2.  Accidents and suicide are also associated with a bigger gap.
3.  More alcohol-related deaths among men are associated with a bigger gap.
4.  Poorer countries have lower life expectancy for both sexes, but in the Baltics men fall further below the pattern than women do.
5.  Where women are much more educated than men, the gap is bigger.
6.  The gap has narrowed in most countries since 2015, but not at the same speed.
7.  These factors overlap. Some may only stand in for wealth or for alcohol, so the analysis checks which of them still matters when the others are taken into account.

## Main findings

This part is written last, after Section 6, so that a reader sees the answer before the method. The expected message above stays unchanged, and the found message is placed next to it.

|   | Message |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Expected** (written before the data) | Baltic men die earlier, and this goes mainly with heart disease deaths before 65. |
| **Found** (written after Section 6) | *To be written.* |

## The pipeline

The analysis runs as one chain. Each step uses only the output of the step before it.

```         
Five Eurostat tables                                    (Section 2)
  life expectancy, healthy life years, deaths by cause, GDP, education
  saved untouched to data/raw/
        ↓
Cleaning                                                (Section 3)
  five data quality checks per table, then documented decisions
  only the 27 EU member states are kept
        ↓
Combining                                               (Section 4)
  women and men side by side, the gap computed
  joined on country code and year
  → data/clean/gap_panel.csv, one row per country and year (about 270 rows)
        ↓
Exploration                                             (Section 5)
  the gap against each candidate factor, the gap over time,
  the Baltic states against the rest of the EU
        ↓
The story                                               (Section 6)
  one chart, built up in five frames
  → figures/story_frame_1.png to story_frame_5.png
```

# 1. Environment setup

This section prepares R before any data is loaded. It has to be run first, every time the project is opened. Every later section depends on it.

**Two steps:**

1.  **Packages:** load the R packages used in the analysis, and install any that are missing.
2.  **Project folder:** check that R finds the project folder, so every file path works on any computer.

## 1.1 Packages

All packages are loaded here, at the start, so they are listed in one place. `pacman::p_load()` loads each package and installs it first if it is missing. This way the file also runs on a computer that has never seen this project.

| Package | Purpose in the analysis |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `tidyverse` | Reading files (`read_csv()`), working with tables (`filter()`, `mutate()`, joins, pivots) and charts (`ggplot()`) |
| `here` | File paths that start at the project folder, for example `here("data", "raw", "demo_mlexpec.csv")` |
| `janitor` | `clean_names()`, which makes column names short, lowercase and easy to type |
| `gtsummary` | `tbl_summary()`, a ready-made table of missing values and ranges for the data quality checks |
| `knitr` | `kable()`, which turns a small result table into a neat table in the rendered report. Not taught in the course, used only for display |
| `scales` | Readable axis labels, for example `label_percent()` for the education shares |
| `ggrepel` | Country labels on charts that push away from each other, so they do not overlap (`geom_text_repel()`) |
| `patchwork` | Places several charts side by side or on top of each other, for example a weak and an improved version of the same chart (`p1 + p2`). Not taught in the course |

```{r}
#| label: setup
# 1.1 Load every package the analysis uses, installing any that are missing
pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse,   # read_csv(), dplyr verbs, pivots, joins, ggplot2
  here,        # file paths that start at the project folder
  janitor,     # clean_names()
  gtsummary,   # tbl_summary() for the data quality tables
  knitr,       # kable() for neat result tables
  scales,     # axis labels such as percentages
  ggrepel,     # country labels that don't overlap
  patchwork    # several charts side by side, for example p1 + p2
)
```

**What it shows:** nothing if all goes well. A message only appears if a package had to be installed.

`here()` finds the project folder by looking for the project file `final_project.Rproj` (or the empty `.here` file) in it. All paths start from there, so no full path like `C:/Users/...` is needed, and the project also works on another computer. The folders follow the course's final project template.

| Folder | Content |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `data/raw/` | The downloads from Eurostat, exactly as they arrived. These files are never edited. `SOURCE.md` lists where each one comes from |
| `data/clean/` | The clean tables created in the analysis |
| `figures/` | Exported charts |
| `notes/` | Decisions made during the analysis and a glossary of functions |

```{r}
#| label: show-here
# 1.2 Check where R thinks the project folder is
here()  # should end in Final_work
```

**What it shows:** the path to the project folder. If it ends somewhere else, the `.here` file is missing.

# 2. Gathering data

To answer the research question, the analysis needs comparable figures for every EU country on life expectancy, health, causes of death, wealth and education, for the same years. The natural source is Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU. It collects the same figures from every member state using the same definitions, so the countries can be compared.

The data is not downloaded by hand from the Eurostat website. Each table is requested from Eurostat's API (a web address that returns data) directly from R, so anyone can rerun this file and get the same data. Every Eurostat table has a code, for example `demo_mlexpec`, and is split into dimensions: sex, age, country, year. The values needed are selected inside the download link.

Every dataset is loaded in its **original, uncleaned form**. The only selection happens in the download link (sex, age, years), where it is visible to any reader. After the download, nothing is filtered, renamed or fixed in this section. Cleaning while loading would hide what was removed. Keeping gathering (Section 2) and cleaning (Section 3) apart means that every dropped row is a documented decision, not a side effect of the loading step.

**Every dataset follows the same three steps:**

1.  **Build the link:** the table code plus the selected dimensions.
2.  **Download once:** save the file to `data/raw/`. This folder is never edited, so the original download is always available.
3.  **Load and look:** read the file into R, check its structure with `glimpse()` and inspect the first rows with `head()`.

**Naming of objects:** every object created for a dataset starts with the full name of that dataset, followed by what the object holds. The names are long, but they say exactly what each object is. For life expectancy the prefix is `life_expectancy_`: `life_expectancy_url` (the download link), `life_expectancy_file` (the path to the saved file), `life_expectancy_raw` (the table as downloaded) and, in Section 3, `life_expectancy_clean` (the cleaned table). The other datasets follow the same pattern: `healthy_life_years_`, `deaths_`, `gdp_` and `education_`.

| Sub-section | Dataset | Eurostat code | Role in the analysis |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| 2.1 | Life expectancy at birth | `demo_mlexpec` | The gap between women and men, the main measure |
| 2.2 | Healthy life years | `hlth_hlye` | Years in good health, women and men |
| 2.3 | Deaths by cause | `hlth_cd_asdr2` | Death rates under 65 by cause, including alcohol-related causes |
| 2.4 | GDP per capita | `tec00114` | Wealth of each country compared with the EU average |
| 2.5 | Education by sex | `sdg_04_20` | Share of 25 to 34 year olds with a university degree |

**The EU member states.** The analysis covers the 27 EU member states. Their codes are defined once, here, because they are used in two places: in the download link of the deaths table (2.3) and in the cleaning of every table (Section 3). Eurostat writes Greece as `EL`, not `GR`.

```{r}
#| label: show-eu-codes
# 2. The 27 EU member states, in Eurostat's codes (Greece is EL)
eu_codes <- c("AT", "BE", "BG", "CY", "CZ", "DE", "DK", "EE", "EL",   # one code per member state
              "ES", "FI", "FR", "HR", "HU", "IE", "IT", "LT", "LU",
              "LV", "MT", "NL", "PL", "PT", "RO", "SE", "SI", "SK")

length(eu_codes)   # should be 27
```

**What it shows:** the number 27, one code per member state.

## 2.1 Life expectancy at birth

|  |  |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Eurostat code** | `demo_mlexpec`, "Life expectancy by age and sex" |
| **What it measures** | How many years a newborn would live on average, if the death rates of that year stayed the same for their whole life |
| **Unit** | Years |
| **Selected dimensions** | Sex: `F` (females) and `M` (males). Age: `Y_LT1` ("less than 1 year"), which is how Eurostat labels life expectancy at birth. All countries, years 2015 to 2024 |
| **Flags** | Some values carry letters: `e` estimated, `p` provisional, `b` break in the series (the method changed that year) |

**Role in the analysis:** this is the main measure. The gap is women's life expectancy minus men's, so this table provides the value on the y axis of most charts.

**Points to note:**

- Life expectancy is a snapshot, not a forecast. It does not follow real people through life. It answers the question: "if the current death rates never changed, how long would a baby born now live?"
- The table has 97 age classes, from `Y_LT1` to `Y_GE95`. Without selecting `Y_LT1` in the link, the file would have 97 rows per country, sex and year instead of one.
- The file also contains EU totals and non-EU countries. They are kept for now and removed in Section 3.
- 2020 and 2021 show a COVID dip. This is real, not an error.

### 2.1.1 Build the link

The link has four parts: the API address, the table code, the selected dimensions, and the years. In the dimension part, dots separate the dimensions in this order: frequency, unit, sex, age, country. `F+M` means both sexes, and the empty position after the last dot means all countries.

```{r}
#| label: show-life-expectancy-url
# 2.1.1 The Eurostat API link for life expectancy
life_expectancy_url <- paste0(
  "https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/api/dissemination/sdmx/2.1/data/",  # the API address
  "demo_mlexpec/",                      # the table code
  "A.YR.F+M.Y_LT1.",                    # annual, in years, women and men, at birth, all countries
  "?startPeriod=2015&endPeriod=2024",   # the study period
  "&format=SDMX-CSV"                    # ask for a CSV file
)

life_expectancy_url  # print the link, so it can also be opened in a browser
```

**What it shows:** one long web address. Pasted into a browser, it downloads the same CSV file.

### 2.1.2 Download once

The file is saved to `data/raw/`. The `if` check makes R download only when the file is not there yet, so rerunning this document never overwrites the original download.

```{r}
#| label: show-life-expectancy-download
# 2.1.2 Save the raw file to data/raw/, only if it isn't there yet
life_expectancy_file <- here("data", "raw", "demo_mlexpec.csv")  # where the raw file goes

if (!file.exists(life_expectancy_file)) {   # TRUE only on the first run
  download.file(life_expectancy_url,        # from this link
                life_expectancy_file,       # to this file
                mode = "wb")                # "wb" copies the file byte for byte
}
```

**What it shows:** on the first run, a short message with the file size. After that, nothing, because the file already exists.

### 2.1.3 Load and look

Eurostat writes missing values as `:`, so `read_csv()` is told to treat `:` as missing. This is not cleaning: the values stay missing, R only reads them correctly. The column names stay exactly as Eurostat wrote them, for example `TIME_PERIOD` and `OBS_VALUE`.

```{r}
#| label: show-life-expectancy-load
# 2.1.3 Read the raw file and check what arrived
life_expectancy_raw <- read_csv(life_expectancy_file,
                                na = c("", ":", "NA"),   # Eurostat marks missing values with ":"
                                show_col_types = FALSE)  # keep the output short

glimpse(life_expectancy_raw)  # rows, columns and the type of each column
```

`glimpse()` lists every column with its type. `head()` shows the first rows as a table, the way the file is actually laid out.

```{r}
#| label: show-life-expectancy-head
# 2.1.3 The first six rows of the raw table
head(life_expectancy_raw)   # how the file is laid out: one row per country, sex and year
```

**What it shows:** a first overview of the raw table. Size and column types are visible in the output above. The remaining points are verified with code in Section 3.1.

- **Size:** 906 rows and 11 columns.
- **One row** is one geographic unit, one sex and one year, with its life expectancy in `OBS_VALUE`.
- **Types:** `OBS_VALUE` and `TIME_PERIOD` are numbers, so the flags did not turn the values into text. `CONF_STATUS` is empty in every row.
- **Geographic units:** 53 codes. They include all 27 EU member states (Greece appears as `EL`, not `GR`), 9 aggregates such as `EU27_2020`, `EA20` and `DE_TOT`, and 17 non-EU countries such as `NO`, `UK` and `UA`.
- **Completeness:** every EU member state has all 10 years for both sexes (27 × 2 × 10 = 540 rows). Some non-EU countries have fewer years.
- **Missing values and flags:** no value in `OBS_VALUE` is missing. 146 values carry a flag in `OBS_FLAG` (estimated, provisional or a break in the series).
- **Columns with one value only:** `freq`, `unit` and `age` repeat the choices made in the link, so they add no information. They are removed in Section 3.

## 2.2 Healthy life years

|  |  |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Eurostat code** | `hlth_hlye`, "Healthy life years and life expectancy at birth, by sex" |
| **What it measures** | How many years a newborn would live in good health, without limitations in daily activities, if the conditions of that year stayed the same |
| **Unit** | Years |
| **Selected dimensions** | Unit: `YR` (years). Sex: `F` and `M`. Indicator: `HLY_Y0`, healthy life years at birth. All countries, years 2015 to 2024 |

**Role in the analysis:** life expectancy says how long people live. Healthy life years say how much of that life is spent in good health. Together they show whether Baltic men lose years of life, years of good health, or both.

### 2.2.1 Build the link

The link has the same four parts as in 2.1. The dimensions are different in this table: frequency, unit, sex, health indicator, country. The table holds nine indicators (healthy life years and life expectancy, at birth, at 50 and at 65, in years and as a share), so the link selects only `HLY_Y0`.

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-url
# 2.2.1 The Eurostat API link for healthy life years
healthy_life_years_url <- paste0(
  "https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/api/dissemination/sdmx/2.1/data/",  # the API address
  "hlth_hlye/",                         # the table code
  "A.YR.F+M.HLY_Y0.",                   # annual, in years, women and men, healthy life years at birth, all countries
  "?startPeriod=2015&endPeriod=2024",   # the study period
  "&format=SDMX-CSV"                    # ask for a CSV file
)

healthy_life_years_url  # print the link, so it can also be opened in a browser
```

**What it shows:** one long web address. Pasted into a browser, it downloads the same CSV file.

### 2.2.2 Download once

Same as in 2.1.2: the file is saved to `data/raw/`, and only if it is not there yet.

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-download
# 2.2.2 Save the raw file to data/raw/, only if it isn't there yet
healthy_life_years_file <- here("data", "raw", "hlth_hlye.csv")  # where the raw file goes

if (!file.exists(healthy_life_years_file)) {   # TRUE only on the first run
  download.file(healthy_life_years_url,        # from this link
                healthy_life_years_file,       # to this file
                mode = "wb")                   # "wb" copies the file byte for byte
}
```

**What it shows:** on the first run, a short message with the file size. After that, nothing, because the file already exists.

### 2.2.3 Load and look

Same as in 2.1.3: `:` is read as a missing value, and the column names stay exactly as Eurostat wrote them.

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-load
# 2.2.3 Read the raw file and check what arrived
healthy_life_years_raw <- read_csv(healthy_life_years_file,
                                   na = c("", ":", "NA"),   # Eurostat marks missing values with ":"
                                   show_col_types = FALSE)  # keep the output short

glimpse(healthy_life_years_raw)  # rows, columns and the type of each column
```

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-head
# 2.2.3 The first six rows of the raw table
head(healthy_life_years_raw)   # how the file is laid out: one row per country, sex and year
```

**What it shows:** a first overview of the raw table. The remaining points are verified with code in Section 3.2.

- **Size:** 618 rows and 11 columns.
- **One row** is one geographic unit, one sex and one year, with its healthy life years in `OBS_VALUE`.
- **Types:** `OBS_VALUE` and `TIME_PERIOD` are numbers (`<dbl>`), so the flags did not turn the values into text.
- **Columns:** the same as in the life expectancy table, except that `age` is replaced by `hlth_hle`, the health indicator. It holds `HLY_Y0` in every row, as selected in the link.
- **Geographic units:** 33 codes, far fewer than the 53 in the life expectancy table. They are the 27 EU member states, 4 non-EU countries (`CH`, `IS`, `NO`, `UK`) and 2 aggregates (`EU27_2020`, `EU28`).
- **Completeness:** 26 of the 27 EU member states have all 10 years for both sexes. Luxembourg has no values for 2023 and 2024, so the EU part has 536 rows instead of 540.
- **Missing values:** no value in `OBS_VALUE` is missing. Missing years appear as missing rows, not as empty cells, so `summary()` alone would not reveal them. Only the row counts do.
- **Flags:** 80 values carry a flag, most often `b` (a break in the series). In the EU, the two Lithuanian values for 2024 are marked `p` (provisional), the only flags in the Baltic states.

## 2.3 Deaths by cause

|  |  |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Eurostat code** | `hlth_cd_asdr2`, "Causes of death, standardised death rate by NUTS 2 region of residence" |
| **What it measures** | How many people per 100 000 die of a given cause in a year, age-standardised |
| **Unit** | `RT`: deaths per 100 000 inhabitants |
| **Selected dimensions** | Sex: `F` and `M`. Age: `Y_LT65` (under 65). Cause: all 93. Countries: the 27 EU member states. Years 2015 to 2024 (the table currently ends in 2023) |

**Role in the analysis:** this table tests the main hypothesis. If Baltic men die earlier mainly because of heart disease before 65, it shows up here as a much higher death rate from circulatory diseases among men than among women.

**Points to note:**

- **Age-standardised** means the rates are calculated as if every country had the same age structure. Without it, a country with many older people would always look worse. With it, the countries can be compared fairly.
- **Under 65 only.** Deaths before 65 are the ones that pull life expectancy down most, and they are where the gap between women and men is expected to come from.
- **All 93 causes are downloaded.** Choosing only the causes named in the hypotheses could hide a cause that was not expected, which would bias the analysis by design. The analysis first looks at the big, non-overlapping groups of causes (chapters such as circulatory diseases, cancer or external causes) without choosing anything, and only then at the specific causes named in the hypotheses.
- **Causes are nested.** Some causes are part of others, for example ischaemic heart disease (`I20-I25`) is part of all circulatory diseases (`I`). They can be compared, but never added up.
- **The 27 EU countries are selected in the link,** unlike in 2.1 and 2.2. Besides 36 countries, the table holds about 460 regions, so the full file would be 55 MB. Only the countries are needed.
- **The latest year is 2023.** Death statistics take longer to publish than life expectancy.

### 2.3.1 Build the link

The same four parts as in 2.1 and 2.2. The dimensions of this table, in order: frequency, unit, sex, age, cause of death, country. The cause position is left empty, which means all causes. The country position lists the 27 EU codes joined with `+`.

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-url
# 2.3.1 The Eurostat API link for deaths by cause
deaths_url <- paste0(
  "https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/api/dissemination/sdmx/2.1/data/",  # the API address
  "hlth_cd_asdr2/",                     # the table code
  "A.RT.F+M.Y_LT65..",                  # annual, rate per 100 000, women and men, under 65, all causes (empty)
  paste(eu_codes, collapse = "+"),      # the 27 EU countries, joined as AT+BE+BG+...
  "?startPeriod=2015&endPeriod=2024",   # the study period
  "&format=SDMX-CSV"                    # ask for a CSV file
)

deaths_url  # print the link, so it can also be opened in a browser
```

**What it shows:** one long web address, with the 27 country codes near the end.

### 2.3.2 Download once

Same as in 2.1.2, with one extra check. For larger requests, Eurostat sometimes puts the request in a queue and sends back a short waiting message instead of the data. Saved as a file, that message would look like a CSV but hold no data. A real Eurostat CSV always starts with the column name `DATAFLOW`, so the first line of the file is checked. If it is anything else, the file is deleted and the chunk stops with a message to run it again a minute later.

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-download
# 2.3.2 Save the raw file to data/raw/, only if it isn't there yet
deaths_file <- here("data", "raw", "hlth_cd_asdr2.csv")  # where the raw file goes

if (!file.exists(deaths_file)) {             # TRUE only on the first run
  download.file(deaths_url,                  # from this link
                deaths_file,                 # to this file
                mode = "wb")                 # "wb" copies the file byte for byte

  first_line <- readLines(deaths_file, n = 1)            # read only the first line of the file
  if (!startsWith(first_line, "DATAFLOW")) {             # a real Eurostat CSV starts with DATAFLOW
    file.remove(deaths_file)                             # delete the waiting message, keep data/raw/ clean
    stop("Eurostat queued the request. Wait a minute and run this chunk again.")   # stop with a clear message
  }
}
```

**What it shows:** on the first run, a short message with the file size. After that, nothing, because the file already exists. If Eurostat queued the request, a red message says to run the chunk again.

### 2.3.3 Load and look

Same as in 2.1.3 and 2.2.3: `:` is read as a missing value, and the column names stay exactly as Eurostat wrote them. This table has one column more than the first two: `icd10`, the cause of death, coded with the international classification of diseases (ICD-10).

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-load
# 2.3.3 Read the raw file and check what arrived
deaths_raw <- read_csv(deaths_file,
                       na = c("", ":", "NA"),   # Eurostat marks missing values with ":"
                       show_col_types = FALSE)  # keep the output short

glimpse(deaths_raw)  # rows, columns and the type of each column
```

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-head
# 2.3.3 The first six rows of the raw table
head(deaths_raw)   # how the file is laid out: one row per country, sex, cause and year
```

**What it shows:** a first overview of the raw table. The remaining points are verified with code in Section 3.3.

- **Size:** 43 902 rows and 12 columns.
- **One row** is one country, one sex, one cause and one year, with its death rate per 100 000 in `OBS_VALUE`.
- **Columns:** the same as in the first two tables, plus `icd10`, the cause of death.
- **Countries:** exactly the 27 EU member states, as asked in the link, each with 1 626 rows.
- **Years:** 2015 to 2023. There is no 2024 yet.
- **Causes:** 93 codes, but not all in every year. 89 codes exist from 2015 to 2019, and 92 from 2020, when three COVID-19 codes were added.
- **"All causes" has two codes.** The total of all causes is coded `TOTAL` in 2015 to 2017 and 2022 to 2023, but `A-R_V-Y` in 2018 to 2021. It is the same measure under two names, so it has to be handled in cleaning, otherwise the total would seem to disappear in four years.
- **Missing values and flags:** no value is missing and no value carries a flag. `OBS_FLAG` and `CONF_STATUS` are empty in every row.
- **Range:** from 0 (causes with no deaths under 65 in a small country) to 716.9 deaths per 100 000.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2.4 GDP per capita

|  |  |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Eurostat code** | `tec00114`, "GDP per capita in PPS" |
| **What it measures** | How rich a country is per person, compared with the EU average |
| **Unit** | Index, EU27 = 100. A value of 120 means 20% above the EU average, 70 means 30% below |
| **Selected dimensions** | Indicator: `VI_PPS_EU27_2020_HAB` (volume index per person, in purchasing power standards). Category: `GDP`. All countries, years 2015 to 2024 |

**Role in the analysis:** wealth is the factor that could explain everything else. Poorer countries may have lower life expectancy for both sexes, and the analysis checks whether the Baltic gap is larger than their income alone would suggest (hypothesis 4).

**Points to note:**

- **PPS (purchasing power standards)** removes the differences in price levels between countries. A euro buys more in Bulgaria than in Luxembourg, and PPS corrects for that, so the countries can be compared fairly.
- **No sex dimension.** GDP is a figure for the whole country, so there is one value per country and year, not one for women and one for men.
- **An index compares countries, not years.** Over time it shows whether a country catches up with the EU average or falls behind, not whether it grows in real terms.
- **The file also contains non-EU countries** such as Norway, the United States and Japan, and aggregates such as the euro area. As in 2.1 and 2.2, they are kept for now and removed in Section 3. The file is small, so the 30 October rule (EU filter in cleaning) applies again.

### 2.4.1 Build the link

The same four parts as before. This table has four dimensions: frequency, indicator, category and country. The country position is left empty, which means all countries.

```{r}
#| label: show-gdp-url
# 2.4.1 The Eurostat API link for GDP per capita
gdp_url <- paste0(
  "https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/api/dissemination/sdmx/2.1/data/",  # the API address
  "tec00114/",                          # the table code
  "A.VI_PPS_EU27_2020_HAB.GDP.",        # annual, volume index per person (EU27 = 100), GDP, all countries
  "?startPeriod=2015&endPeriod=2024",   # the study period
  "&format=SDMX-CSV"                    # ask for a CSV file
)

gdp_url  # print the link, so it can also be opened in a browser
```

**What it shows:** one long web address. Pasted into a browser, it downloads the same CSV file.

### 2.4.2 Download once

Same as in 2.3.2, including the check of the first line. The file is small, so Eurostat is not expected to queue it, but the check costs nothing and protects `data/raw/` in case it does.

```{r}
#| label: show-gdp-download
# 2.4.2 Save the raw file to data/raw/, only if it isn't there yet
gdp_file <- here("data", "raw", "tec00114.csv")   # where the raw file goes

if (!file.exists(gdp_file)) {                    # TRUE only on the first run
  download.file(gdp_url,                         # from this link
                gdp_file,                        # to this file
                mode = "wb")                     # "wb" copies the file byte for byte

  first_line <- readLines(gdp_file, n = 1)                # read only the first line of the file
  if (!startsWith(first_line, "DATAFLOW")) {              # a real Eurostat CSV starts with DATAFLOW
    file.remove(gdp_file)                                 # delete the waiting message, keep data/raw/ clean
    stop("Eurostat queued the request. Wait a minute and run this chunk again.")   # stop with a clear message
  }
}
```

**What it shows:** on the first run, a short message with the file size. After that, nothing, because the file already exists.

### 2.4.3 Load and look

Same as in 2.1.3 to 2.3.3. This table has no `sex` column, and two columns that describe the indicator: `indic_ppp` and `ppp_cat18`.

```{r}
#| label: show-gdp-load
# 2.4.3 Read the raw file and check what arrived
gdp_raw <- read_csv(gdp_file,
                    na = c("", ":", "NA"),   # Eurostat marks missing values with ":"
                    show_col_types = FALSE)  # keep the output short

glimpse(gdp_raw)  # rows, columns and the type of each column
```

```{r}
#| label: show-gdp-head
# 2.4.3 The first six rows of the raw table
head(gdp_raw)   # how the file is laid out: one row per country and year
```

**What it shows:** a first overview of the raw table. The remaining points are verified with code in Section 3.4.

- **Size:** 430 rows and 10 columns, one fewer than the first two tables, because there is no `sex` column.
- **One row** is one geographic unit and one year, with its GDP index in `OBS_VALUE`. There is no `sex` column.
- **Geographic units:** 43 codes: the 27 EU member states, the aggregates `EU27_2020`, `EA19`, `EA20` and `EA21` (the euro area in different years), and 12 other countries such as `NO`, `UK`, `US` and `JP`.
- **Completeness:** every unit has all 10 years, so the EU part has 270 rows (27 × 10).
- **Missing values and flags:** no value is missing. 9 values are marked `p` (provisional), all from 2023 or 2024. In the EU these are Germany, Greece and Spain in 2023 and 2024, and France in 2024. The Baltic states have no flags.
- **Range in the EU:** from 49 (Bulgaria, 2015) to 279 (Luxembourg, 2015). Luxembourg is far above every other country, partly because many people work there but live in neighbouring countries, so its GDP is shared by fewer residents.

## 2.5 Education by sex

|  |  |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Eurostat code** | `sdg_04_20`, "Tertiary educational attainment" |
| **What it measures** | The share of people aged 25 to 34 who have finished tertiary education (a university degree or a similar higher education) |
| **Unit** | Percent of the age group |
| **Selected dimensions** | Sex: `F` and `M`. Age: `Y25-34`. Unit: `PC` (percentage). Education level: `ED5-8` (tertiary, levels 5 to 8). All countries, years 2015 to 2024 |

**Role in the analysis:** this table tests hypothesis 5: where women are much more educated than men, the gap in life expectancy is bigger. Education goes with income, health habits and the kind of work people do, so a large difference in education between women and men may go with a large difference in how long they live.

**Points to note:**

- **Ages 25 to 34 only.** This is the age when most people have finished their studies. It describes the young generation, not the people who die before 65 today, so it is a sign of how the country is changing rather than a cause of today's deaths.
- **ED5-8** covers all tertiary levels: short tertiary courses, bachelor, master and doctorate.
- **The file also contains non-EU countries and aggregates.** As in 2.1, 2.2 and 2.4, they are kept for now and removed in Section 3. The file is small, so the 30 October rule (EU filter in cleaning) applies.

### 2.5.1 Build the link

This table has six dimensions: frequency, sex, age, unit, education level and country. The country position is left empty, which means all countries.

```{r}
#| label: show-education-url
# 2.5.1 The Eurostat API link for tertiary education by sex
education_url <- paste0(
  "https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/api/dissemination/sdmx/2.1/data/",  # the API address
  "sdg_04_20/",                         # the table code
  "A.F+M.Y25-34.PC.ED5-8.",             # annual, women and men, age 25 to 34, percent, tertiary, all countries
  "?startPeriod=2015&endPeriod=2024",   # the study period
  "&format=SDMX-CSV"                    # ask for a CSV file
)

education_url  # print the link, so it can also be opened in a browser
```

**What it shows:** one long web address. Pasted into a browser, it downloads the same CSV file.

### 2.5.2 Download once

Same as in 2.3.2 and 2.4.2, including the check of the first line.

```{r}
#| label: show-education-download
# 2.5.2 Save the raw file to data/raw/, only if it isn't there yet
education_file <- here("data", "raw", "sdg_04_20.csv")   # where the raw file goes

if (!file.exists(education_file)) {              # TRUE only on the first run
  download.file(education_url,                   # from this link
                education_file,                  # to this file
                mode = "wb")                     # "wb" copies the file byte for byte

  first_line <- readLines(education_file, n = 1)          # read only the first line of the file
  if (!startsWith(first_line, "DATAFLOW")) {              # a real Eurostat CSV starts with DATAFLOW
    file.remove(education_file)                           # delete the waiting message, keep data/raw/ clean
    stop("Eurostat queued the request. Wait a minute and run this chunk again.")   # stop with a clear message
  }
}
```

**What it shows:** on the first run, a short message with the file size. After that, nothing, because the file already exists.

### 2.5.3 Load and look

Same as in the other four tables.

```{r}
#| label: show-education-load
# 2.5.3 Read the raw file and check what arrived
education_raw <- read_csv(education_file,
                          na = c("", ":", "NA"),   # Eurostat marks missing values with ":"
                          show_col_types = FALSE)  # keep the output short

glimpse(education_raw)  # rows, columns and the type of each column
```

```{r}
#| label: show-education-head
# 2.5.3 The first six rows of the raw table
head(education_raw)   # how the file is laid out: one row per country, sex and year
```

**What it shows:** a first overview of the raw table. The remaining points are verified with code in Section 3.5.

- **Size:** 730 rows and 12 columns.
- **One row** is one geographic unit, one sex and one year, with the share of 25 to 34 year olds with tertiary education in `OBS_VALUE`.
- **Geographic units:** 38 codes: the 27 EU member states, the aggregates `EU27_2020` and `EA21`, and 9 other countries such as `NO`, `UK` and `RS`.
- **Completeness:** all 27 EU member states have all 10 years for both sexes (540 rows). Three non-EU units have fewer: `UK` (10 rows), `ME` (12) and `BA` (8).
- **Missing values:** none.
- **Flags:** 104 values are marked `b` (break in the series), 72 of them in 2021, when the EU changed the method of its labour force survey, the source of this table. 3 values for Luxembourg (2016 and 2017) are marked `u` (low reliability), which in a survey usually means the sample was small.
- **Range in the EU:** from 19.4% (Italian men, 2015) to 70.8% (Cypriot women, 2023).

# 3. Cleaning

This section checks the quality of every raw table before anything is removed or changed. Only after the checks are the cleaning decisions made, so each decision is based on what the data actually contains.

The first step for every table is `clean_names()`, which turns Eurostat's column names like `TIME_PERIOD` into `time_period`. It is done here, not during loading, so the raw tables in Section 2 keep Eurostat's original names.

Every table then goes through the same five data quality checks, taken from the course checklist (class 03, "Know your data"):

| \# | Check | Question | Function |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| 1 | Types | Is every column the type it should be, for example numbers stored as numbers? | `glimpse()` |
| 2 | Missing values | How many values are missing, and where? | `tbl_summary()`, `count()` |
| 3 | Units and ranges | Are the values plausible for the unit? | `geom_histogram()` with `facet_wrap()` |
| 4 | Duplicates | Does any combination of country, sex and year appear twice? | `distinct()`, `nrow()` |
| 5 | Row counts | Does each country have the expected number of rows? | `count()`, `geom_col()` |

Short result tables are shown with `kable()` from `knitr`, which turns a table into a neat table in the rendered report. It changes only how a table looks, never the data.

Each sub-section ends with a short summary table: what each check found, and what was decided because of it.

| Sub-section | Dataset                  | Clean object               |
|-------------|--------------------------|----------------------------|
| 3.1         | Life expectancy at birth | `life_expectancy_clean`    |
| 3.2         | Healthy life years       | `healthy_life_years_clean` |
| 3.3         | Deaths by cause          | `deaths_clean`             |
| 3.4         | GDP per capita           | `gdp_clean`                |
| 3.5         | Education by sex         | `education_clean`          |

**The EU member states.** Every table in this section is checked and filtered with the same list of 27 member state codes, `eu_codes`, defined at the start of Section 2.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3.1 Life expectancy at birth

The life expectancy table goes through four stages. Nothing is removed until the checks are done and the decisions are written down.

| Stage | What happens | Result |
|------------------|------------------------------------|------------------|
| 3.1.1 | Tidy the column names | Readable names, same data |
| 3.1.2 | Run the five quality checks | One result per check |
| 3.1.3 | Summarise what was found and decide | A table of decisions |
| 3.1.4 | Apply the decisions | `life_expectancy_clean`, EU only, key columns only |

### 3.1.1 Tidy the column names

Eurostat uses the same technical column names in every table: `geo` for the country, `time_period` for the year and `obs_value` ("observed value") for the number itself. Two steps make them readable. `clean_names()` first turns them into lowercase with underscores, so `LAST UPDATE`, which contains a space, becomes `last_update`. `rename()` then gives the four key columns names that say what they hold. The new names `country_code` and `year` are also the keys used to join the tables in Section 4.

| Eurostat name | After `clean_names()` | After `rename()`  |
|---------------|-----------------------|-------------------|
| `geo`         | `geo`                 | `country_code`    |
| `TIME_PERIOD` | `time_period`         | `year`            |
| `OBS_VALUE`   | `obs_value`           | `life_expectancy` |
| `OBS_FLAG`    | `obs_flag`            | `flag`            |

```{r}
#| label: show-life-expectancy-names
# 3.1.1 Make the column names readable
life_expectancy_clean <- life_expectancy_raw |>   # start from the untouched raw table
  clean_names() |>                        # for example TIME_PERIOD becomes time_period
  rename(country_code    = geo,           # new name = old name
         year            = time_period,   # the year, a key for the join in Section 4
         life_expectancy = obs_value,     # the value: life expectancy at birth
         flag            = obs_flag)      # e, p, b ... how the value was produced

names(life_expectancy_clean)   # list the new column names
```

**What it shows:** the same 11 columns. Four of them have new names: `country_code`, `year`, `life_expectancy` and `flag`. The technical columns (`dataflow`, `last_update`, `freq`, `unit`, `age`, `conf_status`) keep their names for now and are removed after the checks.

### 3.1.2 The five quality checks

The checks run on all 906 rows, before anything is removed, so that problems outside the EU are also visible.

#### Check 1: types

`glimpse()` lists every column with its type: `<dbl>` for numbers, `<chr>` for text and `<lgl>` for logical (`TRUE`/`FALSE`). The value column must be a number. If an Eurostat flag had been written into the same cell as the value, for example `75.2 e`, R would read the whole column as text. The check runs again here, on the renamed table, so that every check of Section 3 can be read in one place.

```{r}
#| label: show-life-expectancy-types
# 3.1.2 Check 1: the type of every column
glimpse(life_expectancy_clean)   # life_expectancy and year should be <dbl>
```

**Result:** `life_expectancy` and `year` are numbers. All other columns are text, except `conf_status`, which R reads as logical because it is empty.

#### Check 2: missing values

`tbl_summary()` from `gtsummary` (class 04) puts the two key columns in one table: the spread of `life_expectancy` and the number of rows for each `sex`. `missing = "always"` adds a "Missing" row to every variable, even when the count is 0, so the table shows that missing values were checked, not only that none were reported.

```{r}
#| label: show-life-expectancy-missing
# 3.1.2 Check 2: missing values and spread of the key columns
life_expectancy_clean |>
  tbl_summary(
    include   = c(life_expectancy, sex),                 # the two columns to check
    type      = life_expectancy ~ "continuous2",         # show the number on several lines
    statistic = life_expectancy ~ c("{median} ({p25} to {p75})",   # middle half
                                    "{min} to {max}"),             # full range
    label     = list(life_expectancy ~ "Life expectancy at birth (years)",   # readable row names
                     sex ~ "Sex"),
    missing      = "always",                             # a Missing row, even if it is 0
    missing_text = "Missing"                             # the word shown in that row
  )
```

The `flag` column is left out of that table, because in `flag` an empty cell means "no flag", not a missing value. Its letters are counted separately, and `kable()` shows the result as a table.

```{r}
#| label: show-life-expectancy-flags
# 3.1.2 Check 2: how many values carry a flag, and which one
life_expectancy_clean |>
  count(flag, sort = TRUE) |>                     # most common flag first
  kable(col.names = c("Flag", "Number of values"))  # NA here means "no flag"
```

**Result:** no value of `life_expectancy` is missing. `sex` holds only `F` and `M`, with 453 rows each, so there are no gaps. 146 of the 906 values carry a flag, most often `b` (66 values, a break in the series), then `e` (28), `ep` (16), `bep` (12), `be` (10), `p` (10) and `bp` (4). A flag marks how a value was produced, not a missing value, so every flagged value is kept. Most flags belong to countries outside the focus: in the 27 EU member states only 52 of 540 values carry a flag, and Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have none. `conf_status` is empty in all 906 rows.

#### Check 3: units and ranges

Life expectancy at birth in Europe is expected to lie roughly between 65 and 90 years. A value far outside this range would point to an error, for example a wrong age class. Women and men are drawn in separate panels with `facet_wrap()`, because their values are known to differ, and two dashed lines from `geom_vline()` mark the expected range. The colours come from `viridis`, the course's default palette, which stays readable for people with colour blindness and in black-and-white print.

```{r}
#| label: show-life-expectancy-range
#| fig-height: 4
# 3.1.2 Check 3: the distribution of life expectancy values, women and men apart
life_expectancy_clean |>
  ggplot(aes(x = life_expectancy, fill = sex)) +     # one number, so a histogram (class 10_1)
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1,
                 color = "white") +                  # one bar per year, white gaps between bars
  scale_fill_viridis_d(begin = 0.25, end = 0.75) +   # course palette: blue for women, green for men
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(65, 90),
             linetype = "dashed") +                  # the expected range
  facet_wrap(~ sex,
             labeller = as_labeller(c(F = "Women", M = "Men"))) +   # one panel per sex
  labs(title = "All values lie inside the expected range of 65 to 90 years",   # the title states the finding
       x = "Life expectancy at birth (years)",
       y = "Number of rows") +
  theme_minimal() +                                  # white background, light grid
  theme(legend.position = "none",                    # the panel titles already name the sexes
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())          # fewer lines that carry no data
```

**Result:** the values run from 66.8 to 86.5 years, all inside the expected range of 65 to 90. Half of the rows lie between 78.1 and 83.5 years (the middle line of the table in Check 2). No value points to a wrong age class or a wrong unit.

#### Check 4: duplicates

Each combination of country, sex and year should appear only once. If the number of distinct combinations equals the number of rows, no row repeats.

```{r}
#| label: show-life-expectancy-duplicates
# 3.1.2 Check 4: compare all rows with distinct country, sex and year combinations
nrow(life_expectancy_clean)   # all rows

life_expectancy_clean |>
  distinct(country_code, sex, year) |>   # each combination once
  nrow()
```

**Result:** both counts are 906. Every combination of country, sex and year appears exactly once, so the table has no duplicates.

#### Check 5: row counts

With 10 years and 2 sexes, every geographic unit should have 20 rows. `count()` gives the number of rows per unit, and a bar chart shows all 53 units at once (class 10_2). `fct_reorder()` sorts the bars by length, `coord_flip()` turns them sideways so the codes are readable, and `geom_hline()` draws the expected 20 rows as a line. EU member states are orange and all other units purple, from the `plasma` palette of the viridis family. Red is not used here, because in this project it is kept for the Baltic states.

```{r}
#| label: show-life-expectancy-rows
#| fig-height: 9
# 3.1.2 Check 5: number of rows per geographic unit, EU member states in orange
life_expectancy_clean |>
  count(country_code) |>                                  # n = number of rows per unit
  mutate(eu = country_code %in% eu_codes,                 # TRUE for the 27 member states
         country_code = fct_reorder(country_code, n)) |>  # sort the bars by n
  ggplot(aes(x = country_code, y = n, fill = eu)) +      # one bar per unit, coloured by EU or not
  geom_col() +                                            # bar length = the number of rows
  geom_hline(yintercept = 20, linetype = "dashed") +      # the expected 20 rows
  coord_flip() +                                          # bars sideways, codes readable
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "plasma",
                       begin = 0.15, end = 0.75,                    # purple and orange, no red
                       labels = c("Other unit", "EU member state"), # FALSE comes first, then TRUE
                       name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Every EU member state has all 20 rows",   # the title states the finding
       x = NULL,                                         # the country codes need no axis title
       y = "Number of rows (expected: 20)") +
  theme_minimal() +                                  # white background, light grid
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())              # the bars need no horizontal grid
```

The EU member states are the focus of the analysis, so their completeness is checked separately, with the `eu_codes` list from the start of Section 3. This only counts the rows. Nothing is removed yet.

```{r}
#| label: show-life-expectancy-eu-rows
# 3.1.2 Check 5: count the rows of the EU member states, without removing anything
life_expectancy_clean |>
  filter(country_code %in% eu_codes) |>   # look at the member states only
  nrow()                                  # expected: 27 x 2 x 10 = 540
```

Finally, the columns `freq`, `unit` and `age` should each hold only one value, because they were fixed in the download link.

```{r}
#| label: show-life-expectancy-constant
# 3.1.2 Check 5: columns fixed in the link: each should have only one value
life_expectancy_clean |>
  distinct(freq, unit, age) |>   # one row means each column has one value
  kable()                        # show the result as a neat table
```

**Result:** all 27 EU member states have the full 20 rows, 540 rows together, as expected. The units with fewer than 20 rows are all outside the focus: non-EU countries such as `XK` (2 rows), `MD` (6) and `UK` (8), and old aggregates such as `EU28` and `EU27_2007` (8 each). `freq`, `unit` and `age` each hold a single value (`A`, `YR`, `Y_LT1`), so they carry no information and can be removed.

### 3.1.3 Summary: what was found, what was decided

| Check | What was found | Decision |
|-----------------|----------------------------|----------------------------|
| 1 Types | `life_expectancy` and `year` are numbers, the flags did not turn them into text | No change needed |
| 2 Missing values | No missing values. 146 of 906 values carry a flag, none in the Baltic states | Flagged values are kept |
| 3 Units and ranges | 66.8 to 86.5 years, all inside the expected range | No change needed |
| 4 Duplicates | Every country, sex and year appears once | No change needed |
| 5 Row counts | All 27 EU member states complete (540 rows). The incomplete units are all non-EU countries or aggregates | Only the 27 EU member states are kept, using `eu_codes` |
| 5 Columns fixed in the link | `freq`, `unit` and `age` hold one value each. `conf_status` is empty. `dataflow` and `last_update` describe the download, not the data | These six technical columns are removed. The `last_update` date is reported once, in the source line |

After these decisions, `life_expectancy_clean` keeps five columns: `country_code`, `sex`, `year`, `life_expectancy` and `flag`. The `flag` column stays, so that estimated or provisional values can still be recognised later, for example when an outlier is checked in Section 5.

### 3.1.4 Apply the decisions

The decisions from 3.1.3 are applied in two steps, and the row count is checked after each one.

#### Keep only the EU member states

`filter()` keeps only the rows whose country code is in `eu_codes`. This removes the non-EU countries, such as `NO` and `UK`, and the aggregates, such as `EU27_2020` and `EA20`. The aggregates would otherwise count every country twice: once on its own and once inside the EU total.

```{r}
#| label: show-life-expectancy-eu
# 3.1.4 Keep only the 27 EU member states
nrow(life_expectancy_clean)   # before: 906 rows

life_expectancy_clean <- life_expectancy_clean |>
  filter(country_code %in% eu_codes)   # drop non-EU countries and aggregates such as EU27_2020

nrow(life_expectancy_clean)   # after: expected 27 x 2 x 10 = 540
```

**What it shows:** 906 rows before and 540 after. The 366 removed rows are the non-EU countries and the aggregates.

#### Remove the technical columns

`select()` keeps only the columns that are listed, in the order they are listed. Naming the five columns to keep, instead of the six to drop, makes the final table visible in the code itself.

```{r}
#| label: show-life-expectancy-select
# 3.1.4 Keep the five columns the analysis uses
life_expectancy_clean <- life_expectancy_clean |>
  select(country_code, sex, year, life_expectancy, flag)   # everything else is dropped

glimpse(life_expectancy_clean)   # expected: 540 rows, 5 columns
```

**What it shows:** the clean table, with 540 rows and 5 columns. `country_code`, `sex` and `flag` are text, `year` and `life_expectancy` are numbers. This is the life expectancy table that goes into Section 4.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3.2 Healthy life years

The healthy life years table goes through the same four stages as the life expectancy table in 3.1. The code follows the same pattern, so only what is new is explained in detail. The first look in 2.2.3 already showed one new problem: Luxembourg has no values for 2023 and 2024.

| Stage | What happens | Result |
|------------------|------------------------------------|------------------|
| 3.2.1 | Tidy the column names | Readable names, same data |
| 3.2.2 | Run the five quality checks | One result per check |
| 3.2.3 | Summarise what was found and decide, including Luxembourg | A table of decisions |
| 3.2.4 | Apply the decisions | `healthy_life_years_clean`, EU only, key columns only |

### 3.2.1 Tidy the column names

Same as in 3.1.1: `clean_names()` makes every name lowercase with underscores, and `rename()` gives the four key columns names that say what they hold. The value column becomes `healthy_life_years`. The column `hlth_hle` (the health indicator, `HLY_Y0` in every row) takes the place of `age` in the life expectancy table and keeps its name until it is removed in 3.2.4.

| Eurostat name | After `clean_names()` | After `rename()`     |
|---------------|-----------------------|----------------------|
| `geo`         | `geo`                 | `country_code`       |
| `TIME_PERIOD` | `time_period`         | `year`               |
| `OBS_VALUE`   | `obs_value`           | `healthy_life_years` |
| `OBS_FLAG`    | `obs_flag`            | `flag`               |

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-names
# 3.2.1 Make the column names readable
healthy_life_years_clean <- healthy_life_years_raw |>   # start from the untouched raw table
  clean_names() |>                                      # for example TIME_PERIOD becomes time_period
  rename(country_code       = geo,                      # new name = old name
         year               = time_period,              # the year, a key for the join in Section 4
         healthy_life_years = obs_value,                # the value: healthy life years at birth
         flag               = obs_flag)                 # e, p, b ... how the value was produced

names(healthy_life_years_clean)   # list the new column names, expected: 11
```

**What it shows:** the same 11 columns. Four of them have new names: `country_code`, `year`, `healthy_life_years` and `flag`. The technical columns (`dataflow`, `last_update`, `freq`, `unit`, `hlth_hle`, `conf_status`) keep their names for now and are removed after the checks.

### 3.2.2 The five quality checks

The checks run on all 618 rows, before anything is removed. The code is the same as in 3.1.2, applied to the new table. Two things differ: healthy life years are lower than life expectancy, so the expected range is different, and one EU member state is incomplete, which Check 5 is built to show.

#### Check 1: types

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-types
# 3.2.2 Check 1: the type of every column
glimpse(healthy_life_years_clean)   # healthy_life_years and year should be <dbl>
```

**Result:** `healthy_life_years` and `year` are numbers. All other columns are text, except `conf_status`, which R reads as logical because it is empty.

#### Check 2: missing values

The same two tables as in 3.1.2: `tbl_summary()` for the value and `sex`, and a separate count of the flags.

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-missing
# 3.2.2 Check 2: missing values and spread of the key columns
healthy_life_years_clean |>                                  # the renamed table, all 618 rows
  tbl_summary(
    include   = c(healthy_life_years, sex),                  # the two columns to check
    type      = healthy_life_years ~ "continuous2",          # show the number on several lines
    statistic = healthy_life_years ~ c("{median} ({p25} to {p75})",   # middle half
                                       "{min} to {max}"),             # full range
    label     = list(healthy_life_years ~ "Healthy life years at birth", # readable row names
                     sex ~ "Sex"),
    missing      = "always",                                 # a Missing row, even if it is 0
    missing_text = "Missing"                                 # the word shown in that row
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-flags
# 3.2.2 Check 2: how many values carry a flag, and which one
healthy_life_years_clean |>                         # the renamed table, all 618 rows
  count(flag, sort = TRUE) |>                       # most common flag first
  kable(col.names = c("Flag", "Number of values"))  # NA here means "no flag"
```

This table has one flag letter that the life expectancy table did not have: `u`, which Eurostat uses for "low reliability". It appears together with `b` as `bu`.

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-low-reliability
# 3.2.2 Check 2: which values are marked as low reliability (u)
healthy_life_years_clean |>                              # the renamed table, all 618 rows
  filter(str_detect(flag, "u")) |>                       # keep rows whose flag contains the letter u
  select(country_code, sex, year, healthy_life_years, flag) |>   # only the columns worth reading
  kable()                                                # show the result as a neat table
```

**Result:** no value of `healthy_life_years` is missing, and the median is 62.5 years. `sex` holds only `F` and `M`, with 309 rows each. "Missing 0" only covers empty cells. Years that are absent from the file, as for Luxembourg, are not counted here and only appear in the row counts of Check 5. 80 of the 618 values carry a flag, most often `b` (56 values, a break in the series), then `p` (8), `e` (4), `bp` (4), `be` (2), `bep` (2), `bu` (2) and `ep` (2). As in 3.1, flagged values are kept. The only values marked as low reliability are the two German values for 2022 (61.2 years for women, 60.9 for men). Germany is not a focus country, but a jump for Germany in 2022 in Section 5 has to be read with this flag in mind. In the EU, 70 of 536 values carry a flag. In the Baltic states only the two Lithuanian values for 2024 do, marked `p` (provisional). `conf_status` is empty in all 618 rows.

#### Check 3: units and ranges

Healthy life years are always fewer than total life expectancy, because they count only the years without limitations in daily activities. In the EU they are expected to lie roughly between 45 and 80 years. A value outside this range would point to an error, for example a wrong indicator.

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-range
#| fig-height: 4
# 3.2.2 Check 3: the distribution of healthy life years, women and men apart
healthy_life_years_clean |>
  ggplot(aes(x = healthy_life_years, fill = sex)) +  # one number, so a histogram (class 10_1)
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1,
                 color = "white") +                  # one bar per year, white gaps between bars
  scale_fill_viridis_d(begin = 0.25, end = 0.75) +   # same colours as in 3.1: blue women, green men
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(45, 80),
             linetype = "dashed") +                  # the expected range
  facet_wrap(~ sex,
             labeller = as_labeller(c(F = "Women", M = "Men"))) +   # one panel per sex
  labs(title = "All values lie inside the expected range of 45 to 80 years",   # the title states the finding
       x = "Healthy life years at birth",
       y = "Number of rows") +
  theme_minimal() +                                  # white background, light grid
  theme(legend.position = "none",                    # the panel titles already name the sexes
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())          # fewer lines that carry no data
```

**Result:** the values run from 50.6 to 74.6 years, all inside the expected range of 45 to 80. The lowest value in the whole table belongs to Latvian men in 2017. No value points to a wrong indicator or a wrong unit.

#### Check 4: duplicates

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-duplicates
# 3.2.2 Check 4: compare all rows with distinct country, sex and year combinations
nrow(healthy_life_years_clean)            # all rows, expected: 618

healthy_life_years_clean |>
  distinct(country_code, sex, year) |>    # each combination once
  nrow()                                  # the same number means no duplicates
```

**Result:** both counts are 618. Every combination of country, sex and year appears exactly once, so the table has no duplicates.

#### Check 5: row counts

The same bar chart as in 3.1.2. Every unit should have 20 rows (10 years, 2 sexes). This is the check where the missing years of Luxembourg become visible.

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-rows
#| fig-height: 6
# 3.2.2 Check 5: number of rows per geographic unit, EU member states in orange
healthy_life_years_clean |>
  count(country_code) |>                                  # n = number of rows per unit
  mutate(eu = country_code %in% eu_codes,                 # TRUE for the 27 member states
         country_code = fct_reorder(country_code, n)) |>  # sort the bars by n
  ggplot(aes(x = country_code, y = n, fill = eu)) +      # one bar per unit, coloured by EU or not
  geom_col() +                                            # bar length = the number of rows
  geom_hline(yintercept = 20, linetype = "dashed") +      # the expected 20 rows
  coord_flip() +                                          # bars sideways, codes readable
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "plasma",
                       begin = 0.15, end = 0.75,                    # purple and orange, no red
                       labels = c("Other unit", "EU member state"), # FALSE comes first, then TRUE
                       name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "26 of 27 EU member states have all 20 rows",   # the title states the finding
       x = NULL,                                         # the country codes need no axis title
       y = "Number of rows (expected: 20)") +
  theme_minimal() +                                       # white background, light grid
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())              # the bars need no horizontal grid
```

The incomplete EU member state is looked at more closely: which years and which sex are missing?

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-luxembourg
# 3.2.2 Check 5: the years that Luxembourg has, for each sex
healthy_life_years_clean |>
  filter(country_code == "LU") |>     # Luxembourg only
  count(sex, year) |>                 # one row per sex and year that exists
  count(sex, name = "years") |>       # how many years each sex has, expected: 10
  kable()                             # show the result as a neat table
```

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-eu-rows
# 3.2.2 Check 5: count the rows of the EU member states, without removing anything
healthy_life_years_clean |>
  filter(country_code %in% eu_codes) |>   # look at the member states only
  nrow()                                  # a complete table would have 27 x 2 x 10 = 540
```

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-constant
# 3.2.2 Check 5: columns fixed in the link: each should have only one value
healthy_life_years_clean |>
  distinct(freq, unit, hlth_hle) |>   # one row means each column has one value
  kable()                             # show the result as a neat table
```

**Result:** 26 of the 27 EU member states have the full 20 rows. Luxembourg has 16: 8 years for each sex, with 2023 and 2024 missing for both. The EU part of the table therefore has 536 rows instead of 540. The other incomplete units are all outside the focus: `NO` (18 rows, 2021 missing), `IS`, `UK` and the old aggregate `EU28` (8 each). `freq`, `unit` and `hlth_hle` each hold a single value (`A`, `YR`, `HLY_Y0`), so they carry no information and can be removed.

### 3.2.3 Summary: what was found, what was decided

| Check | What was found | Decision |
|-----------------|----------------------------|----------------------------|
| 1 Types | `healthy_life_years` and `year` are numbers, the flags did not turn them into text | No change needed |
| 2 Missing values | No empty cells. 80 of 618 values carry a flag. Germany's two values for 2022 are marked low reliability (`bu`). In the Baltic states only Lithuania's 2024 values carry a flag (`p`) | Flagged values are kept, as in 3.1. The German 2022 values are kept and noted for Section 5 |
| 3 Units and ranges | 50.6 to 74.6 years, all inside the expected range of 45 to 80 | No change needed |
| 4 Duplicates | Every country, sex and year appears once | No change needed |
| 5 Row counts | 26 of 27 EU member states complete. Luxembourg has no values for 2023 and 2024 (536 EU rows instead of 540) | Only the 27 EU member states are kept, using `eu_codes`. Luxembourg is kept with its 16 real values. Its 2023 and 2024 stay missing and are not filled in |
| 5 Columns fixed in the link | `freq`, `unit` and `hlth_hle` hold one value each. `conf_status` is empty. `dataflow` and `last_update` describe the download, not the data | These six technical columns are removed. The `last_update` date is reported once, in the source line |

After these decisions, `healthy_life_years_clean` keeps five columns: `country_code`, `sex`, `year`, `healthy_life_years` and `flag`, the same structure as `life_expectancy_clean`.

**Why Luxembourg is kept.** Three options were considered: keep Luxembourg with the two missing years, drop Luxembourg from this table, or shorten the period to 2015 to 2022 for every country. Dropping Luxembourg would discard 16 real values to avoid 4 missing ones. Shortening the period would remove the two most recent years for all 27 countries, including the Baltic states. Keeping Luxembourg loses no real data and invents none. After the join in Section 4, its healthy life years for 2023 and 2024 appear as `NA`, and the gap is named in Section 7.

### 3.2.4 Apply the decisions

The same two steps as in 3.1.4, with the row count checked after each one.

#### Keep only the EU member states

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-eu
# 3.2.4 Keep only the 27 EU member states
nrow(healthy_life_years_clean)   # before: 618 rows

healthy_life_years_clean <- healthy_life_years_clean |>   # overwrite the table with the filtered version
  filter(country_code %in% eu_codes)                      # drop non-EU countries and aggregates such as EU27_2020

nrow(healthy_life_years_clean)   # after: expected 536 (540 minus Luxembourg's 4 missing rows)
```

**What it shows:** 618 rows before and 536 after. The 82 removed rows are the non-EU countries and the aggregates. The count is 536, not 540, because Luxembourg's 2023 and 2024 were never in the file.

#### Remove the technical columns

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-select
# 3.2.4 Keep the five columns the analysis uses
healthy_life_years_clean <- healthy_life_years_clean |>             # overwrite the table again
  select(country_code, sex, year, healthy_life_years, flag)         # everything else is dropped

glimpse(healthy_life_years_clean)   # expected: 536 rows, 5 columns
```

**What it shows:** the clean table, with 536 rows and 5 columns, the same five columns as `life_expectancy_clean` except for the name of the value column. This is the healthy life years table that goes into Section 4.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3.3 Deaths by cause

The deaths table goes through the same four stages as the first two tables. It is larger and has one more dimension, the cause of death, so the checks also look at the causes. The first look in 2.3.3 already showed one new problem: "all causes" is coded `TOTAL` in some years and `A-R_V-Y` in others.

| Stage | What happens | Result |
|------------------|------------------------------------|------------------|
| 3.3.1 | Tidy the column names | Readable names, same data |
| 3.3.2 | Run the five quality checks | One result per check |
| 3.3.3 | Summarise what was found and decide, including the two "all causes" codes and the chapters of causes | A table of decisions |
| 3.3.4 | Apply the decisions | `deaths_clean` |

### 3.3.1 Tidy the column names

Same as in 3.1.1 and 3.2.1. The value column becomes `death_rate`. The extra column `icd10` becomes `cause_code`, because it holds the code of the cause of death, and the name should say what it holds, not which classification system it comes from.

| Eurostat name | After `clean_names()` | After `rename()` |
|---------------|-----------------------|------------------|
| `geo`         | `geo`                 | `country_code`   |
| `TIME_PERIOD` | `time_period`         | `year`           |
| `icd10`       | `icd10`               | `cause_code`     |
| `OBS_VALUE`   | `obs_value`           | `death_rate`     |
| `OBS_FLAG`    | `obs_flag`            | `flag`           |

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-names
# 3.3.1 Make the column names readable
deaths_clean <- deaths_raw |>                  # start from the untouched raw table
  clean_names() |>                             # for example TIME_PERIOD becomes time_period
  rename(country_code = geo,                   # new name = old name
         year         = time_period,           # the year, a key for the join in Section 4
         cause_code   = icd10,                 # the ICD-10 code of the cause of death
         death_rate   = obs_value,             # the value: deaths per 100 000, under 65
         flag         = obs_flag)              # e, p, b ... how the value was produced

names(deaths_clean)   # list the new column names, expected: 12
```

**What it shows:** the same 12 columns. Five of them have new names: `country_code`, `year`, `cause_code`, `death_rate` and `flag`.

### 3.3.2 The five quality checks

The checks run on all 43 902 rows, before anything is removed. The code follows 3.1.2 and 3.2.2. What is new: the countries were already limited to the EU in the download link, and there is one more dimension to check, the cause of death.

#### Check 1: types

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-types
# 3.3.2 Check 1: the type of every column
glimpse(deaths_clean)   # death_rate and year should be <dbl>
```

**Result:** `death_rate` and `year` are numbers. `country_code`, `sex` and `cause_code` are text. `flag` and `conf_status` are read as logical, because they are empty in every row.

#### Check 2: missing values

The same two tables as before: `tbl_summary()` for the value and `sex`, and a count of the flags.

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-missing
# 3.3.2 Check 2: missing values and spread of the key columns
deaths_clean |>                                          # the renamed table, all 43 902 rows
  tbl_summary(
    include   = c(death_rate, sex),                      # the two columns to check
    type      = death_rate ~ "continuous2",              # show the number on several lines
    statistic = death_rate ~ c("{median} ({p25} to {p75})",   # middle half
                               "{min} to {max}"),             # full range
    label     = list(death_rate ~ "Death rate under 65 (per 100 000)",   # readable row names
                     sex ~ "Sex"),
    missing      = "always",                             # a Missing row, even if it is 0
    missing_text = "Missing"                             # the word shown in that row
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-flags
# 3.3.2 Check 2: how many values carry a flag, and which one
deaths_clean |>                                     # the renamed table, all 43 902 rows
  count(flag, sort = TRUE) |>                       # most common flag first
  kable(col.names = c("Flag", "Number of values"))  # NA here means "no flag"
```

**Result:** no value of `death_rate` is missing, and `sex` holds only `F` and `M`, with 21 951 rows each. No value carries a flag. The median death rate is only 1.7 per 100 000, and half of all values lie between 0.4 and 5.2, because most of the 93 causes are rare: 3 151 values are exactly 0 (no deaths from that cause under 65 in that country and year). The few large values belong to the broad groups such as all causes or circulatory diseases. A zero is a real count, not a missing value, so it is kept.

#### Check 3: units and ranges

A histogram of all 43 902 values would mix rare causes, close to 0, with the broad groups, in the hundreds, and show little. The range check therefore looks at the one value that must be plausible in every country and year: the death rate from all causes. It is coded `TOTAL` in some years and `A-R_V-Y` in others (see 2.3.3), so both codes are kept here. Under 65, the death rate from all causes in the EU is expected to lie roughly between 50 and 1 000 per 100 000.

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-range
#| fig-height: 4
# 3.3.2 Check 3: the distribution of the death rate from all causes, women and men apart
deaths_clean |>
  filter(cause_code %in% c("TOTAL", "A-R_V-Y")) |>  # all causes, under both of its codes
  ggplot(aes(x = death_rate, fill = sex)) +          # one number, so a histogram (class 10_1)
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 25,
                 color = "white") +                  # one bar per 25 deaths, white gaps between bars
  scale_fill_viridis_d(begin = 0.25, end = 0.75) +   # same colours as before: blue women, green men
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(50, 1000),
             linetype = "dashed") +                  # the expected range
  facet_wrap(~ sex,
             labeller = as_labeller(c(F = "Women", M = "Men"))) +   # one panel per sex
  labs(title = "Death rates from all causes lie inside the expected range",   # the title states the finding
       x = "Deaths from all causes under 65, per 100 000",
       y = "Number of rows") +
  theme_minimal() +                                  # white background, light grid
  theme(legend.position = "none",                    # the panel titles already name the sexes
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())          # fewer lines that carry no data
```

**Result:** all 486 values (27 countries, 2 sexes, 9 years) lie inside the expected range. For women they run from 83 to 320 deaths per 100 000, for men from 146 to 717. The highest value is Latvian men in 2021, a COVID-19 year. The men's panel has a second group of values between about 350 and 700: in some countries, men under 65 die at two to three times the rate of men elsewhere. Which countries these are is examined in Section 5.

#### Check 4: duplicates

In this table, one row should be one country, one sex, one cause and one year. The cause is part of the combination now, because every country, sex and year appears once for each cause.

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-duplicates
# 3.3.2 Check 4: compare all rows with distinct country, sex, cause and year combinations
nrow(deaths_clean)                                  # all rows, expected: 43 902

deaths_clean |>
  distinct(country_code, sex, cause_code, year) |>  # each combination once
  nrow()                                            # the same number means no duplicates
```

**Result:** both counts are 43 902. Every combination of country, sex, cause and year appears exactly once, so the table has no duplicates.

#### Check 5: row counts

The 27 countries were selected in the download link, so the bar chart from 3.1.2 and 3.2.2 would only show 27 equal bars. Here the row counts answer four other questions: does every country have the same number of rows, how many causes exist in each year, which code holds "all causes" in each year, and do the columns fixed in the link hold one value each.

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-rows-per-country
# 3.3.2 Check 5: does every country have the same number of rows?
deaths_clean |>
  count(country_code) |>            # n = number of rows per country
  count(n, name = "countries") |>   # how many countries have each row count
  kable(col.names = c("Rows per country", "Number of countries"))   # one line means all equal
```

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-causes-per-year
# 3.3.2 Check 5: how many different causes exist in each year?
deaths_clean |>
  distinct(year, cause_code) |>     # each cause once per year
  count(year, name = "causes") |>   # number of causes per year
  kable(col.names = c("Year", "Number of causes"))   # expected: 89 up to 2019, 92 from 2020
```

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-all-causes-codes
# 3.3.2 Check 5: which code holds "all causes" in which year?
deaths_clean |>
  filter(cause_code %in% c("TOTAL", "A-R_V-Y")) |>   # the two codes for all causes
  distinct(year, cause_code) |>                      # one row per year and code
```
