```{r}
  arrange(year) |>                                   # in time order
  kable(col.names = c("Year", "Code for all causes")) # one code per year, never both
```

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-constant
# 3.3.2 Check 5: columns fixed in the link: each should have only one value
deaths_clean |>
  distinct(freq, unit, age) |>   # one row means each column has one value
  kable()                        # show the result as a neat table
```

**Result:** all 27 countries have the same 1 626 rows, so no country is incomplete. Up to 2019 each year has 89 causes, from 2020 it has 92, because three COVID-19 codes were added. Every year has exactly one code for all causes: `TOTAL` in 2015 to 2017 and in 2022 to 2023, `A-R_V-Y` in 2018 to 2021. Never both in the same year, so the two codes can be treated as one without counting anything twice. `freq`, `unit` and `age` each hold a single value (`A`, `RT`, `Y_LT65`), the choices made in the link, so they can be removed.

### 3.3.3 Summary: what was found, what was decided

| Check | What was found | Decision |
|-----------------|----------------------------|----------------------------|
| 1 Types | `death_rate` and `year` are numbers | No change needed |
| 2 Missing values | No empty cells, no flags. 3 151 values are 0, real counts of no deaths | Zeros are kept, as real values |
| 3 Units and ranges | All causes: 83 to 320 per 100 000 for women, 146 to 717 for men, all inside the expected range | No change needed |
| 4 Duplicates | Every country, sex, cause and year appears once | No change needed |
| 5 Row counts | All 27 countries complete (1 626 rows each). 89 causes up to 2019, 92 from 2020 (COVID-19 codes added) | No country is removed. The EU was already selected in the link |
| 5 All causes | Coded `TOTAL` in 2015 to 2017 and 2022 to 2023, `A-R_V-Y` in 2018 to 2021, never both in one year | Both codes are merged into one, `TOTAL`, so all causes has the same code in every year |
| 5 Chapters of causes | 93 causes at three levels: all causes, 17 chapters of the ICD-10 classification (plus 3 COVID-19 codes from 2020), and detailed causes inside the chapters. The chapters and COVID-19 add up to all causes in every country, sex and year (differences below 0.03%, from rounding) | A new column `cause_level` marks each row as "all causes", "chapter" or "detail". All rows are kept |
| 5 Columns fixed in the link | `freq`, `unit` and `age` hold one value each. `conf_status` is empty. `dataflow` and `last_update` describe the download | These six technical columns are removed. The `last_update` date is reported once, in the source line |

**Why the two codes for all causes are merged.** Eurostat renamed the code for all causes in 2018 and changed it back in 2022. It is the same measure under two names. Keeping both would mean that every later filter has to ask for both codes, and forgetting it once would make four years disappear without an error. Dropping all causes would lose the best check that the chapters add up. Since no year has both codes, renaming `A-R_V-Y` to `TOTAL` is safe: no row is lost and nothing is counted twice.

**Why the level of each cause is marked, not split or left for later.** The analysis looks first at the chapters of causes, without choosing any cause, and only then deeper at the causes named in the hypotheses (see 2.3). A column `cause_level` makes both views one `filter()` away, and keeps every row. Splitting the table in two would mean two objects to keep in line, and leaving it to Section 5 would hide the chapter list inside the charts. The three COVID-19 codes count as chapter level, because without them the chapters would not add up to all causes from 2020 on.

### 3.3.4 Apply the decisions

Three steps, each followed by a check.

#### Merge the two codes for all causes

`case_when()` (class 04) goes through the rows and gives each one a value: where the condition on the left is true, it uses the value on the right. `.default = cause_code` keeps every other code as it was.

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-merge-total
# 3.3.4 Give "all causes" the same code, TOTAL, in every year
deaths_clean <- deaths_clean |>                         # overwrite the table with the changed version
  mutate(cause_code = case_when(
    cause_code == "A-R_V-Y" ~ "TOTAL",                  # the 2018 to 2021 code becomes TOTAL
    .default = cause_code                               # every other code stays as it is
  ))

deaths_clean |>
  filter(cause_code %in% c("TOTAL", "A-R_V-Y")) |>     # look for both codes again
  count(cause_code) |>                                  # rows per code
  kable(col.names = c("Code", "Rows"))                  # expected: only TOTAL, 486 rows
```

**What it shows:** only `TOTAL` remains, with 486 rows: 27 countries, 2 sexes and 9 years. All causes now has one code in every year.

#### Mark the level of each cause

The 17 chapters of the ICD-10 classification and the 3 COVID-19 codes are listed once, as `chapter_codes`. `case_when()` then labels every row: `TOTAL` is "all causes", the codes in the list are "chapter", and everything else is "detail".

| Code | Chapter |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `A_B` | Infectious and parasitic diseases |
| `C00-D48` | Neoplasms (cancer and other tumours) |
| `D50-D89` | Diseases of the blood and the immune system |
| `E` | Endocrine, nutritional and metabolic diseases (for example diabetes) |
| `F` | Mental and behavioural disorders (including alcohol and drug use) |
| `G_H` | Diseases of the nervous system and the sense organs |
| `I` | Diseases of the circulatory system (heart and blood vessels) |
| `J` | Diseases of the respiratory system |
| `K` | Diseases of the digestive system (including the liver) |
| `L` | Diseases of the skin |
| `M` | Diseases of the musculoskeletal system |
| `N` | Diseases of the genitourinary system |
| `O` | Pregnancy and childbirth |
| `P` | Conditions from the perinatal period |
| `Q` | Congenital malformations |
| `R` | Ill-defined and unknown causes |
| `V01-Y89` | External causes (accidents, suicide, violence) |
| `U071`, `U072`, `U_COV19_OTH` | COVID-19, from 2020 |

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-cause-level
# 3.3.4 Mark each row as all causes, chapter or detail
chapter_codes <- c("A_B", "C00-D48", "D50-D89", "E", "F", "G_H", "I", "J", "K",   # the 17 ICD-10 chapters
                   "L", "M", "N", "O", "P", "Q", "R", "V01-Y89",
                   "U071", "U072", "U_COV19_OTH")                                 # COVID-19, from 2020

deaths_clean <- deaths_clean |>                          # overwrite the table with the new column
  mutate(cause_level = case_when(
    cause_code == "TOTAL"         ~ "all causes",        # the total of all deaths
    cause_code %in% chapter_codes ~ "chapter",           # the big groups that add up to the total
    .default                      = "detail"             # everything else sits inside a chapter
  ))

deaths_clean |>
  distinct(cause_code, cause_level) |>                   # each cause once
  count(cause_level) |>                                  # how many causes at each level
  kable(col.names = c("Level", "Number of causes"))      # expected: 1, 20 and 71 (92 codes after the merge)
```

**What it shows:** 92 causes in three levels: 1 for all causes, 20 at chapter level (17 chapters and 3 COVID-19 codes) and 71 detailed causes. The chapter view in Section 5 is now one `filter(cause_level == "chapter")` away.

#### Remove the technical columns

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-select
# 3.3.4 Keep the seven columns the analysis uses
deaths_clean <- deaths_clean |>                                                  # overwrite the table again
  select(country_code, sex, year, cause_code, cause_level, death_rate, flag)   # everything else is dropped

glimpse(deaths_clean)   # expected: 43 902 rows, 7 columns
```

**What it shows:** the clean table, with 43 902 rows and 7 columns: the same five columns as the first two tables, plus `cause_code` and `cause_level`. No row was removed in this section. This is the deaths table that goes into Section 4.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3.4 GDP per capita

The GDP table goes through the same four stages. It is the simplest of the five tables: one value per country and year, with no sex and no cause. As in 3.1 and 3.2, the non-EU countries and aggregates are removed in this section.

| Stage | What happens | Result |
|------------------|------------------------------------|------------------|
| 3.4.1 | Tidy the column names | Readable names, same data |
| 3.4.2 | Run the five quality checks | One result per check |
| 3.4.3 | Summarise what was found and decide | A table of decisions |
| 3.4.4 | Apply the decisions | `gdp_clean`, EU only, key columns only |

### 3.4.1 Tidy the column names

Same as before. The value column becomes `gdp_pps_index`: GDP per person, in purchasing power standards, as an index with the EU average at 100. The name is long, but it says what the number is, so it cannot be mistaken for GDP in euros.

| Eurostat name | After `clean_names()` | After `rename()` |
|---------------|-----------------------|------------------|
| `geo`         | `geo`                 | `country_code`   |
| `TIME_PERIOD` | `time_period`         | `year`           |
| `OBS_VALUE`   | `obs_value`           | `gdp_pps_index`  |
| `OBS_FLAG`    | `obs_flag`            | `flag`           |

```{r}
#| label: show-gdp-names
# 3.4.1 Make the column names readable
gdp_clean <- gdp_raw |>                        # start from the untouched raw table
  clean_names() |>                             # for example TIME_PERIOD becomes time_period
  rename(country_code  = geo,                  # new name = old name
         year          = time_period,          # the year, a key for the join in Section 4
         gdp_pps_index = obs_value,            # the value: GDP per person, EU27 = 100
         flag          = obs_flag)             # p = provisional

names(gdp_clean)   # list the new column names, expected: 10
```

**What it shows:** the same 10 columns. Four of them have new names: `country_code`, `year`, `gdp_pps_index` and `flag`.

### 3.4.2 The five quality checks

The checks run on all 430 rows, before anything is removed. The code follows 3.1.2, without `sex`, because GDP is one value per country and year.

#### Check 1: types

```{r}
#| label: show-gdp-types
# 3.4.2 Check 1: the type of every column
glimpse(gdp_clean)   # gdp_pps_index and year should be <dbl>
```

**Result:** `gdp_pps_index` and `year` are numbers. `flag` is text, because 9 rows hold the letter `p`. `conf_status` is read as logical, because it is empty.

#### Check 2: missing values

```{r}
#| label: show-gdp-missing
# 3.4.2 Check 2: missing values and spread of the GDP index
gdp_clean |>                                             # the renamed table, all 430 rows
  tbl_summary(
    include   = gdp_pps_index,                           # the one value column (no sex here)
    type      = gdp_pps_index ~ "continuous2",           # show the number on several lines
    statistic = gdp_pps_index ~ c("{median} ({p25} to {p75})",   # middle half
                                  "{min} to {max}"),             # full range
    label     = gdp_pps_index ~ "GDP per capita in PPS (EU27 = 100)",   # readable row name
    missing      = "always",                             # a Missing row, even if it is 0
    missing_text = "Missing"                             # the word shown in that row
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: show-gdp-flags
# 3.4.2 Check 2: how many values carry a flag, and which one
gdp_clean |>                                        # the renamed table, all 430 rows
  count(flag, sort = TRUE) |>                       # most common flag first
  kable(col.names = c("Flag", "Number of values"))  # NA here means "no flag"
```

**Result:** no value of `gdp_pps_index` is missing. The median is 96, close to the EU average of 100, and half of all values lie between 70 and 118. The full range runs from 30 (Albania, 2015) to 279 (Luxembourg, 2015). 9 values are marked `p` (provisional), all from 2023 or 2024, the most recent years, which Eurostat may still revise. As in the other tables, flagged values are kept.

#### Check 3: units and ranges

An index with the EU average at 100 is expected to lie roughly between 20 and 300 for European countries. A value far outside would point to a wrong indicator, for example GDP in euros instead of an index.

```{r}
#| label: show-gdp-range
#| fig-height: 4
# 3.4.2 Check 3: the distribution of the GDP index
gdp_clean |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdp_pps_index)) +                   # one number, so a histogram (class 10_1)
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10,
                 fill = "#21908C",                   # one colour from the viridis palette (teal)
                 color = "white") +                  # one bar per 10 index points, white gaps
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(20, 300),
             linetype = "dashed") +                  # the expected range
  geom_vline(xintercept = 100) +                     # the EU average, as a solid line
  labs(title = "All values lie inside the expected range of 20 to 300",   # the title states the finding
       x = "GDP per capita in PPS (EU27 = 100)",
       y = "Number of rows") +
  theme_minimal() +                                  # white background, light grid
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())          # fewer lines that carry no data
```

**Result:** all values lie inside the expected range of 20 to 300. Most units are close to the EU average, between about 50 and 140. The long tail on the right belongs to two EU countries and Norway: Luxembourg (244 to 279), Ireland (178 to 237) and Norway in 2021 to 2023 (up to 222, when energy prices were high). Luxembourg is high because many of the people who work there live in neighbouring countries, and Ireland because the profits of large international companies are booked there. Both are real values, but they make these two countries look richer than their residents are. This matters in Section 5: in a scatter plot against GDP, Luxembourg and Ireland will sit far to the right and can pull a trend line.

#### Check 4: duplicates

There is no sex in this table, so one row should be one country and one year.

```{r}
#| label: show-gdp-duplicates
# 3.4.2 Check 4: compare all rows with distinct country and year combinations
nrow(gdp_clean)                        # all rows, expected: 430

gdp_clean |>
  distinct(country_code, year) |>      # each combination once
  nrow()                               # the same number means no duplicates
```

**Result:** both counts are 430. Every combination of country and year appears exactly once, so the table has no duplicates.

#### Check 5: row counts

With 10 years and no sex dimension, every geographic unit should have 10 rows. The same bar chart as in 3.1.2 and 3.2.2.

```{r}
#| label: show-gdp-rows
#| fig-height: 6
# 3.4.2 Check 5: number of rows per geographic unit, EU member states in orange
gdp_clean |>
  count(country_code) |>                                  # n = number of rows per unit
  mutate(eu = country_code %in% eu_codes,                 # TRUE for the 27 member states
         country_code = fct_reorder(country_code, n)) |>  # sort the bars by n
  ggplot(aes(x = country_code, y = n, fill = eu)) +      # one bar per unit, coloured by EU or not
  geom_col() +                                            # bar length = the number of rows
  geom_hline(yintercept = 10, linetype = "dashed") +      # the expected 10 rows
  coord_flip() +                                          # bars sideways, codes readable
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "plasma",
                       begin = 0.15, end = 0.75,                    # purple and orange, no red
                       labels = c("Other unit", "EU member state"), # FALSE comes first, then TRUE
                       name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Every unit has all 10 years",            # the title states the finding
       x = NULL,                                         # the country codes need no axis title
       y = "Number of rows (expected: 10)") +
  theme_minimal() +                                       # white background, light grid
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())              # the bars need no horizontal grid
```

```{r}
#| label: show-gdp-eu-rows
# 3.4.2 Check 5: count the rows of the EU member states, without removing anything
gdp_clean |>
  filter(country_code %in% eu_codes) |>   # look at the member states only
  nrow()                                  # expected: 27 x 10 = 270
```

```{r}
#| label: show-gdp-constant
# 3.4.2 Check 5: columns fixed in the link: each should have only one value
gdp_clean |>
  distinct(freq, indic_ppp, ppp_cat18) |>   # one row means each column has one value
  kable()                                   # show the result as a neat table
```

**Result:** all 43 units have the full 10 rows, so no year is missing anywhere. The 27 EU member states have 270 rows together, as expected. `freq`, `indic_ppp` and `ppp_cat18` each hold a single value (`A`, `VI_PPS_EU27_2020_HAB`, `GDP`), the choices made in the link, so they can be removed.

### 3.4.3 Summary: what was found, what was decided

| Check | What was found | Decision |
|-----------------|----------------------------|----------------------------|
| 1 Types | `gdp_pps_index` and `year` are numbers | No change needed |
| 2 Missing values | No missing values. 9 values marked `p` (provisional), all from 2023 or 2024. None in the Baltic states | Flagged values are kept, as in the other tables |
| 3 Units and ranges | 30 to 279, all inside the expected range. Luxembourg (244 to 279) and Ireland (178 to 237) far above all other EU countries | Both are kept as real values, and flagged for Section 5 |
| 4 Duplicates | Every country and year appears once | No change needed |
| 5 Row counts | All 43 units complete (10 rows each), 270 rows for the EU | Only the 27 EU member states are kept, using `eu_codes` |
| 5 Columns fixed in the link | `freq`, `indic_ppp` and `ppp_cat18` hold one value each. `conf_status` is empty. `dataflow` and `last_update` describe the download | These six technical columns are removed. The `last_update` date is reported once, in the source line |

After these decisions, `gdp_clean` keeps four columns: `country_code`, `year`, `gdp_pps_index` and `flag`. It has no `sex` column, because GDP is one value per country.

**Why Luxembourg and Ireland are kept.** Their GDP index is far above the other EU countries for reasons that say little about how well off their residents are: in Luxembourg many workers live in neighbouring countries, and in Ireland the profits of large international companies are booked there. The values are still correct Eurostat data, so they are not changed or removed. Removing the two countries would also drop them from every other comparison, where their values are ordinary. Instead, every chart against GDP in Section 5 is checked with and without them, and if the trend line changes, both versions are shown.

### 3.4.4 Apply the decisions

The same two steps as in 3.1.4 and 3.2.4, with the row count checked after each one.

#### Keep only the EU member states

```{r}
#| label: show-gdp-eu
# 3.4.4 Keep only the 27 EU member states
nrow(gdp_clean)   # before: 430 rows

gdp_clean <- gdp_clean |>                   # overwrite the table with the filtered version
  filter(country_code %in% eu_codes)        # drop non-EU countries and aggregates such as EU27_2020

nrow(gdp_clean)   # after: expected 27 x 10 = 270
```

**What it shows:** 430 rows before and 270 after. The 160 removed rows are 16 units with 10 years each: the four aggregates (`EU27_2020`, `EA19`, `EA20`, `EA21`) and 12 non-EU countries.

#### Remove the technical columns

```{r}
#| label: show-gdp-select
# 3.4.4 Keep the four columns the analysis uses
gdp_clean <- gdp_clean |>                                   # overwrite the table again
  select(country_code, year, gdp_pps_index, flag)           # everything else is dropped

glimpse(gdp_clean)   # expected: 270 rows, 4 columns
```

**What it shows:** the clean table, with 270 rows and 4 columns: `country_code`, `year`, `gdp_pps_index` and `flag`. One row per EU country and year, with no `sex` column. This is the GDP table that goes into Section 4.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3.5 Education by sex

The education table goes through the same four stages. Its structure is the same as the life expectancy table: one value per country, sex and year. As in 3.1, 3.2 and 3.4, the non-EU countries and aggregates are removed in this section.

| Stage | What happens | Result |
|------------------|------------------------------------|------------------|
| 3.5.1 | Tidy the column names | Readable names, same data |
| 3.5.2 | Run the five quality checks | One result per check |
| 3.5.3 | Summarise what was found and decide | A table of decisions |
| 3.5.4 | Apply the decisions | `education_clean`, EU only, key columns only |

### 3.5.1 Tidy the column names

Same as before. The value column becomes `tertiary_pct`: the percentage of 25 to 34 year olds with tertiary education.

| Eurostat name | After `clean_names()` | After `rename()` |
|---------------|-----------------------|------------------|
| `geo`         | `geo`                 | `country_code`   |
| `TIME_PERIOD` | `time_period`         | `year`           |
| `OBS_VALUE`   | `obs_value`           | `tertiary_pct`   |
| `OBS_FLAG`    | `obs_flag`            | `flag`           |

```{r}
#| label: show-education-names
# 3.5.1 Make the column names readable
education_clean <- education_raw |>            # start from the untouched raw table
  clean_names() |>                             # for example TIME_PERIOD becomes time_period
  rename(country_code = geo,                   # new name = old name
         year         = time_period,           # the year, a key for the join in Section 4
         tertiary_pct = obs_value,             # the value: % of 25 to 34 year olds with tertiary education
         flag         = obs_flag)              # b = break in series, u = low reliability

names(education_clean)   # list the new column names, expected: 12
```

**What it shows:** the same 12 columns. Four of them have new names: `country_code`, `year`, `tertiary_pct` and `flag`.

### 3.5.2 The five quality checks

The checks run on all 730 rows, before anything is removed. The code is the same as in 3.1.2, because the two tables have the same structure.

#### Check 1: types

```{r}
#| label: show-education-types
# 3.5.2 Check 1: the type of every column
glimpse(education_clean)   # tertiary_pct and year should be <dbl>
```

**Result:** `tertiary_pct` and `year` are numbers. `flag` is text, because it holds the letters `b` and `u`. `conf_status` is read as logical, because it is empty.

#### Check 2: missing values

```{r}
#| label: show-education-missing
# 3.5.2 Check 2: missing values and spread of the key columns
education_clean |>                                       # the renamed table, all 730 rows
  tbl_summary(
    include   = c(tertiary_pct, sex),                    # the two columns to check
    type      = tertiary_pct ~ "continuous2",            # show the number on several lines
    statistic = tertiary_pct ~ c("{median} ({p25} to {p75})",   # middle half
                                 "{min} to {max}"),             # full range
    label     = list(tertiary_pct ~ "Tertiary education, age 25 to 34 (%)",   # readable row names
                     sex ~ "Sex"),
    missing      = "always",                             # a Missing row, even if it is 0
    missing_text = "Missing"                             # the word shown in that row
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: show-education-flags
# 3.5.2 Check 2: how many values carry a flag, and which one
education_clean |>                                  # the renamed table, all 730 rows
  count(flag, sort = TRUE) |>                       # most common flag first
  kable(col.names = c("Flag", "Number of values"))  # NA here means "no flag"
```

**Result:** no value of `tertiary_pct` is missing, and `sex` holds only `F` and `M`, with 365 rows each. The median is 41%, and half of all values lie between 34% and 51%. The full range runs from 19% (Italian men, 2015) to 71% (Cypriot women, 2023). 104 values are marked `b` (break in the series), 72 of them in 2021, when the EU changed the method of its labour force survey. 3 values for Luxembourg in 2016 and 2017 are marked `u` (low reliability). As in the other tables, flagged values are kept. The 2021 break means that a jump between 2020 and 2021 can come from the new method, not from real change, which matters when the education gap is looked at over time in Section 5.

#### Check 3: units and ranges

A percentage must lie between 0 and 100. For young adults in Europe, the share with tertiary education is expected to lie roughly between 10% and 80%.

```{r}
#| label: show-education-range
#| fig-height: 4
# 3.5.2 Check 3: the distribution of the tertiary education share, women and men apart
education_clean |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tertiary_pct, fill = sex)) +        # one number, so a histogram (class 10_1)
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2,
                 color = "white") +                  # one bar per 2 percentage points, white gaps
  scale_fill_viridis_d(begin = 0.25, end = 0.75) +   # same colours as before: blue women, green men
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(10, 80),
             linetype = "dashed") +                  # the expected range
  facet_wrap(~ sex,
             labeller = as_labeller(c(F = "Women", M = "Men"))) +   # one panel per sex
  labs(title = "All values lie inside the expected range of 10% to 80%",   # the title states the finding
       x = "Share of 25 to 34 year olds with tertiary education (%)",
       y = "Number of rows") +
  theme_minimal() +                                  # white background, light grid
  theme(legend.position = "none",                    # the panel titles already name the sexes
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())          # fewer lines that carry no data
```

**Result:** all values lie inside the expected range of 10% to 80%. The two panels are clearly shifted: most values for women lie between about 40% and 60%, most values for men between about 25% and 45%. In nearly every country, young women are more likely to have a tertiary degree than young men. How large that difference is, and whether it goes with the life expectancy gap, is examined in Section 5.

#### Check 4: duplicates

```{r}
#| label: show-education-duplicates
# 3.5.2 Check 4: compare all rows with distinct country, sex and year combinations
nrow(education_clean)                        # all rows, expected: 730

education_clean |>
  distinct(country_code, sex, year) |>       # each combination once
  nrow()                                     # the same number means no duplicates
```

**Result:** both counts are 730. Every combination of country, sex and year appears exactly once, so the table has no duplicates.

#### Check 5: row counts

With 10 years and 2 sexes, every unit should have 20 rows. The same bar chart as in 3.1.2.

```{r}
#| label: show-education-rows
#| fig-height: 6
# 3.5.2 Check 5: number of rows per geographic unit, EU member states in orange
education_clean |>
  count(country_code) |>                                  # n = number of rows per unit
  mutate(eu = country_code %in% eu_codes,                 # TRUE for the 27 member states
         country_code = fct_reorder(country_code, n)) |>  # sort the bars by n
  ggplot(aes(x = country_code, y = n, fill = eu)) +      # one bar per unit, coloured by EU or not
  geom_col() +                                            # bar length = the number of rows
  geom_hline(yintercept = 20, linetype = "dashed") +      # the expected 20 rows
  coord_flip() +                                          # bars sideways, codes readable
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "plasma",
                       begin = 0.15, end = 0.75,                    # purple and orange, no red
                       labels = c("Other unit", "EU member state"), # FALSE comes first, then TRUE
                       name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Every EU member state has all 20 rows",   # the title states the finding
       x = NULL,                                         # the country codes need no axis title
       y = "Number of rows (expected: 20)") +
  theme_minimal() +                                       # white background, light grid
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())              # the bars need no horizontal grid
```

```{r}
#| label: show-education-eu-rows
# 3.5.2 Check 5: count the rows of the EU member states, without removing anything
education_clean |>
  filter(country_code %in% eu_codes) |>   # look at the member states only
  nrow()                                  # expected: 27 x 2 x 10 = 540
```

```{r}
#| label: show-education-constant
# 3.5.2 Check 5: columns fixed in the link: each should have only one value
education_clean |>
  distinct(freq, age, unit, isced11) |>   # one row means each column has one value
  kable()                                 # show the result as a neat table
```

**Result:** all 27 EU member states have the full 20 rows, 540 rows together, as expected. The incomplete units are all outside the EU: `ME` (12 rows), `UK` (10, no data after 2019, the year before it left the EU) and `BA` (8). `freq`, `age`, `unit` and `isced11` each hold a single value (`A`, `Y25-34`, `PC`, `ED5-8`), the choices made in the link, so they can be removed.

### 3.5.3 Summary: what was found, what was decided

| Check | What was found | Decision |
|------------------|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| 1 Types | `tertiary_pct` and `year` are numbers | No change needed |
| 2 Missing values | No missing values. 104 values marked `b`, 72 of them in 2021 (new survey method). 3 values for Luxembourg (2016, 2017) marked `u` (low reliability) | Flagged values are kept, as in all tables. The 2021 break is kept in mind when the education gap is followed over time in Section 5 |
| 3 Units and ranges | 19% to 71%, all inside the expected range. Women clearly higher than men | No change needed |
| 4 Duplicates | Every country, sex and year appears once | No change needed |
| 5 Row counts | All 27 EU member states complete (540 rows). The incomplete units are all outside the EU | Only the 27 EU member states are kept, using `eu_codes` |
| 5 Columns fixed in the link | `freq`, `age`, `unit` and `isced11` hold one value each. `conf_status` is empty. `dataflow` and `last_update` describe the download | These six technical columns are removed. The `last_update` date is reported once, in the source line |

No new decision was needed for this table: every finding was already covered by a decision made for an earlier table. After these decisions, `education_clean` keeps five columns: `country_code`, `sex`, `year`, `tertiary_pct` and `flag`, the same structure as `life_expectancy_clean`.

### 3.5.4 Apply the decisions

The same two steps as in 3.1.4, with the row count checked after each one.

#### Keep only the EU member states

```{r}
#| label: show-education-eu
# 3.5.4 Keep only the 27 EU member states
nrow(education_clean)   # before: 730 rows

education_clean <- education_clean |>         # overwrite the table with the filtered version
  filter(country_code %in% eu_codes)          # drop non-EU countries and aggregates such as EU27_2020

nrow(education_clean)   # after: expected 27 x 2 x 10 = 540
```

**What it shows:** 730 rows before and 540 after. The 190 removed rows are the aggregates `EU27_2020` and `EA21` and nine non-EU countries.

#### Remove the technical columns

```{r}
#| label: show-education-select
# 3.5.4 Keep the five columns the analysis uses
education_clean <- education_clean |>                          # overwrite the table again
  select(country_code, sex, year, tertiary_pct, flag)          # everything else is dropped

glimpse(education_clean)   # expected: 540 rows, 5 columns
```

**What it shows:** the clean table, with 540 rows and 5 columns: `country_code`, `sex`, `year`, `tertiary_pct` and `flag`. The same structure as `life_expectancy_clean`. This is the education table that goes into Section 4.

# 4. Combining the tables

This section turns five separate tables into one panel, `gap_panel`, with one row per EU country and year: 27 countries times 10 years, 270 rows. Each column holds one thing known about that country in that year. The research question is about relationships, for example whether a larger gap goes with lower GDP, and a chart can only show such a relationship when both numbers sit in the same row.

Life expectancy is complete for all 27 countries and 10 years, so it is the backbone: every other table is joined onto it. Values that a table does not have, such as the deaths of 2024 or Luxembourg's healthy life years for 2023 and 2024, become `NA` in the panel, never 0.

| Step | What happens | Check |
|------------------|------------------------------------|------------------|
| 4.1 | Put women and men side by side with `pivot_wider()` and compute the gap with `mutate()`, one table at a time | The number of rows halves, the gaps lie in a plausible range |
| 4.2 | Deaths: women and men side by side for every cause (`deaths_by_cause`), and deaths from all causes for the panel | 21 951 rows, then 243 rows for all causes |
| 4.3 | Join the tables on country code and year | 270 rows after every join, `anti_join()` lists what did not match |
| 4.4 | Mark the Baltic states | 30 rows marked |
| 4.5 | Save the panel to `data/clean/gap_panel.csv` | The saved file loads again with the same rows and columns |

The tables arrive here already limited to the 27 EU member states (Section 3) and to the years 2015 to 2024 (the download links in Section 2). The `flag` column is dropped before the tables are reshaped: the flags are counted and described table by table in Section 3, and keeping them would add two flag columns per table to the panel.

## 4.1 Women and men side by side

### 4.1.1 Life expectancy

`pivot_wider()` (class 07) turns the values of one column into column names. Here the column `sex` holds `F` and `M`, so the two rows per country and year, one for women and one for men, become one row with two columns, `F` and `M`. `rename()` then gives them names that say what they hold, and `mutate()` computes the gap: women minus men, in years.

```{r}
#| label: show-life-expectancy-wide
# 4.1.1 Life expectancy: women and men side by side, then the gap
life_expectancy_wide <- life_expectancy_clean |>   # start from the clean table of 3.1
  select(-flag) |>                                 # drop the flags, they are described in Section 3
  pivot_wider(names_from  = sex,                   # the values F and M become column names
              values_from = life_expectancy) |>    # the numbers fill the new columns
  rename(le_women = F,                             # new name = old name
         le_men   = M) |>
  mutate(le_gap = le_women - le_men)               # the gap: women minus men, in years

glimpse(life_expectancy_wide)   # expected: 270 rows, 5 columns
```

**What it shows:** 270 rows, half of the 540 rows of `life_expectancy_clean`, because the two rows per country and year (women and men) became one. Five columns: `country_code`, `year`, `le_women`, `le_men` and `le_gap`.

**Check of the gap.** The gap is the first number in the analysis that is calculated, not downloaded, so it is checked before it is used. Women are expected to live roughly 3 to 11 years longer than men in every EU country. A negative gap would mean that women and men were swapped. The five largest gaps in 2024 are also compared with the press figures quoted in the Background (Latvia 9.8 years, Lithuania 8.6, Estonia 8.5).

```{r}
#| label: show-life-expectancy-gap-check
# 4.1.1 Check: the range of the gap, then the five largest gaps in 2024
life_expectancy_wide |>
  summarise(smallest_gap = min(le_gap),     # expected: around 3, never below 0
            largest_gap  = max(le_gap)) |>  # expected: around 11 at most
  kable(digits = 1)                         # one decimal, as in the data

life_expectancy_wide |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>                   # the latest year
  arrange(desc(le_gap)) |>                  # largest gap first
  head(5) |>                                # the top five countries
  kable(digits = 1)                         # show the result as a neat table
```

**What it shows:** the gap runs from 2.8 to 10.4 years, always positive, so women and men were not swapped. In 2024 the three Baltic states have the largest gaps in the EU: Latvia 9.8 years, Lithuania 8.6 and Estonia 8.3, followed by Romania (7.5) and Poland (7.4). Latvia and Lithuania match the press figures exactly. Estonia is 0.2 years lower than the 8.5 quoted in the press, probably because Eurostat revised the figure after the article was written. The analysis uses the Eurostat data. The table also shows where the gap comes from: Baltic women live about as long as women in Romania or Poland, but Baltic men, especially in Latvia (71.4 years), live shorter lives.

### 4.1.2 Healthy life years

The same three steps as in 4.1.1. The table has 536 rows, not 540, because Luxembourg has no values for 2023 and 2024, so the wide table is expected to have 268 rows. The two missing rows come back as `NA` when the tables are joined in 4.3.

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-wide
# 4.1.2 Healthy life years: women and men side by side, then the gap
healthy_life_years_wide <- healthy_life_years_clean |>   # start from the clean table of 3.2
  select(-flag) |>                                       # drop the flags, they are described in Section 3
  pivot_wider(names_from  = sex,                         # the values F and M become column names
              values_from = healthy_life_years) |>       # the numbers fill the new columns
  rename(hly_women = F,                                  # new name = old name
         hly_men   = M) |>
  mutate(hly_gap = hly_women - hly_men)                  # the gap: women minus men, in healthy years

glimpse(healthy_life_years_wide)   # expected: 268 rows, 5 columns
```

**What it shows:** 268 rows, half of the 536 rows of `healthy_life_years_clean`, and five columns: `country_code`, `year`, `hly_women`, `hly_men` and `hly_gap`. Already in Austria the gap is small and sometimes negative, for example -0.6 in 2017.

**Check of the gap.** Unlike life expectancy, the gap in healthy life years can be negative. Women live longer, but they often spend more of those years with limitations in daily activities, so in some countries men have more healthy years than women. A negative value is therefore not an error. The check looks at the range and at how many country-years have a negative gap.

```{r}
#| label: show-healthy-life-years-gap-check
# 4.1.2 Check: the range of the gap, and how often it is negative
healthy_life_years_wide |>
  summarise(smallest_gap  = min(hly_gap),        # can be below 0: men with more healthy years
            largest_gap   = max(hly_gap),        # expected: a few years at most
            negative_gaps = sum(hly_gap < 0)) |> # number of country-years where men have more healthy years
  kable(digits = 1)                              # one decimal, as in the data

healthy_life_years_wide |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>                        # the latest year
  arrange(desc(hly_gap)) |>                      # largest gap first
  head(5) |>                                     # the top five countries
  kable(digits = 1)                              # show the result as a neat table
```

**What it shows:** the gap in healthy life years runs from -5.0 to 5.4 years. In 76 of the 268 country-years it is negative, so men have more healthy years than women, as expected for this measure. In 2024 the largest gaps are in Lithuania (5.4 years), Bulgaria (4.6), Estonia (3.8), Poland (3.0) and Latvia (2.8). Latvia has the largest gap in life expectancy, but only the fifth largest in healthy life years, because Latvian women also have few healthy years (53.9, the lowest of the five). In the Baltic states, men live both shorter lives and fewer healthy years, but healthy years are low for women too.

### 4.1.3 Education

The same steps once more. The gap is again women minus men, here in percentage points: a gap of 20 means that the share of young women with a tertiary degree is 20 percentage points higher than the share of young men.

```{r}
#| label: show-education-wide
# 4.1.3 Education: women and men side by side, then the gap
education_wide <- education_clean |>                     # start from the clean table of 3.5
  select(-flag) |>                                       # drop the flags, they are described in Section 3
  pivot_wider(names_from  = sex,                         # the values F and M become column names
              values_from = tertiary_pct) |>             # the numbers fill the new columns
  rename(tertiary_women_pct = F,                         # new name = old name
         tertiary_men_pct   = M) |>
  mutate(tertiary_gap = tertiary_women_pct - tertiary_men_pct)   # the gap: women minus men, in percentage points

glimpse(education_wide)   # expected: 270 rows, 5 columns
```

**What it shows:** 270 rows, half of the 540 rows of `education_clean`, and five columns: `country_code`, `year`, `tertiary_women_pct`, `tertiary_men_pct` and `tertiary_gap`. Education is complete for all 27 countries and 10 years.

**Check of the gap.** From Check 3 in 3.5.2, women are expected to be ahead in nearly every country, so the gap should be positive almost everywhere and at most around 30 percentage points.

```{r}
#| label: show-education-gap-check
# 4.1.3 Check: the range of the gap, and the five largest gaps in 2024
education_wide |>
  summarise(smallest_gap  = min(tertiary_gap),         # expected: just above 0
            largest_gap   = max(tertiary_gap),         # expected: around 30 at most
            negative_gaps = sum(tertiary_gap < 0)) |>  # country-years where men are ahead
  kable(digits = 1)                                    # one decimal, as in the data

education_wide |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>                              # the latest year
  arrange(desc(tertiary_gap)) |>                       # largest gap first
  head(5) |>                                           # the top five countries
  kable(digits = 1)                                    # show the result as a neat table
```

**What it shows:** the education gap runs from 1.9 to 28.4 percentage points and is never negative: in every EU country and every year, a larger share of young women than of young men has a tertiary degree. The largest gap of all is Latvia in 2015 (28.4). In 2024 the largest gaps are in Slovenia (23.7), Latvia (22.9), Estonia (21.6), Croatia (20.5) and Slovakia (18.9). Two Baltic states are in the top three, but Slovenia, whose life expectancy gap is much smaller, is first, so a large education gap alone does not come with a large life expectancy gap. Whether the two go together across all countries is examined in Section 5.

## 4.2 Deaths: women and men side by side

The deaths table has 92 causes. Putting every cause into `gap_panel` would add about 180 columns. The deaths are therefore kept in two forms:

- **`deaths_by_cause`:** one row per country, year and cause, with women and men side by side. It is used in Section 5 for the overview of the chapters of causes and for the deeper look at the causes named in the hypotheses.
- **Deaths from all causes** go into `gap_panel`, as one more set of columns for each country and year.

The gap in deaths is defined the other way round from the other gaps: **men minus women**, in deaths per 100 000. Men under 65 die more often, so this way a positive number means, as for life expectancy, that men are worse off. A difference is used instead of a ratio (men divided by women), because a ratio cannot be computed when women have no deaths from a cause, which happens 3 151 times in the data. Both rates are kept, so a ratio can still be calculated where it is useful.

### 4.2.1 Every cause side by side

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-by-cause
# 4.2.1 Deaths: women and men side by side for every cause, then the gap
deaths_by_cause <- deaths_clean |>                 # start from the clean table of 3.3
  select(-flag) |>                                 # drop the flags, the deaths table has none anyway
  pivot_wider(names_from  = sex,                   # the values F and M become column names
              values_from = death_rate) |>         # the numbers fill the new columns
  rename(death_women = F,                          # new name = old name
         death_men   = M) |>
  mutate(death_gap = death_men - death_women)      # the gap: men minus women, deaths per 100 000

glimpse(deaths_by_cause)   # expected: 21 951 rows, 7 columns
```

**What it shows:** 21 951 rows, half of the 43 902 rows of `deaths_clean`, and seven columns: `country_code`, `year`, `cause_code`, `cause_level`, `death_women`, `death_men` and `death_gap`. In 2 992 rows the gap is negative, meaning more women than men die of that cause, for example from breast cancer. For most causes and for all causes together, men die more often.

### 4.2.2 Deaths from all causes, for the panel

From `deaths_by_cause`, only the rows for all causes are kept, and the columns get names that say so. This is the part of the deaths data that goes into `gap_panel`.

```{r}
#| label: show-deaths-all-causes
# 4.2.2 Deaths from all causes, one row per country and year, ready for the join
deaths_all_causes <- deaths_by_cause |>
  filter(cause_level == "all causes") |>                  # only the TOTAL rows
  select(country_code, year,                              # the two keys for the join
         death_all_women = death_women,                   # select() can rename too: new name = old name
         death_all_men   = death_men,
         death_all_gap   = death_gap)

glimpse(deaths_all_causes)   # expected: 243 rows (27 countries x 9 years), 5 columns

deaths_all_causes |>
  summarise(smallest_gap = min(death_all_gap),     # expected: positive, men die more in every country
            largest_gap  = max(death_all_gap)) |>  # expected: a few hundred per 100 000
  kable(digits = 1)                                # one decimal
```

**What it shows:** 243 rows, one per country and year from 2015 to 2023, and five columns. The gap in deaths from all causes is positive everywhere: in every EU country and year, more men than women die before 65. It ranges from 44 more deaths per 100 000 (Netherlands, 2019) to 455 more (Latvia, 2021). The rows are not sorted by year, because the code for all causes was `A-R_V-Y` for 2018 to 2021 before it was merged into `TOTAL`. The order does not matter for the join, which matches rows by country and year, not by position.

## 4.3 Joining the tables

The tables are joined one at a time onto the life expectancy table, with `left_join()` (class 08). `left_join()` keeps every row of the first table and adds the columns of the second where `country_code` and `year` match. Where there is no match, the new columns get `NA`. `inner_join()` was not used, because it keeps only rows that exist in every table: all of 2024 (no deaths data yet) and Luxembourg in 2023 would disappear, 28 of 270 rows, including their life expectancy, the main measure.

After every join, two checks follow. The number of rows must still be 270: more rows would mean that a country and year matched twice. And `anti_join()` lists the rows of the panel that found no partner in the new table, so every `NA` is explained.

### 4.3.1 Healthy life years

```{r}
#| label: show-join-healthy-life-years
# 4.3.1 Add healthy life years to the life expectancy table
gap_panel <- life_expectancy_wide |>                       # the backbone: 270 rows
  left_join(healthy_life_years_wide,                       # add the healthy life years columns
            by = join_by(country_code, year))              # match on country and year

nrow(gap_panel)   # must still be 270

life_expectancy_wide |>
  anti_join(healthy_life_years_wide,                       # rows of the backbone with no partner
            by = join_by(country_code, year)) |>
  select(country_code, year) |>                            # only the keys are needed here
  kable()                                                  # expected: Luxembourg 2023 and 2024
```

**What it shows:** the panel still has 270 rows, so no country and year matched twice. Only two rows found no healthy life years: Luxembourg in 2023 and 2024, the two years missing from the Eurostat table (see 3.2). In these two rows, `hly_women`, `hly_men` and `hly_gap` are `NA`.

### 4.3.2 GDP per capita

GDP has no `sex`, so it joins on `country_code` and `year` like the others, and the same GDP value sits next to the values for women and men.

```{r}
#| label: show-join-gdp
# 4.3.2 Add GDP per capita
gap_panel <- gap_panel |>                                  # the panel so far
  left_join(gdp_clean |> select(-flag),                    # GDP without its flag column
            by = join_by(country_code, year))              # match on country and year

nrow(gap_panel)   # must still be 270

gap_panel |>
  anti_join(gdp_clean, by = join_by(country_code, year)) |>   # rows with no GDP
  nrow()                                                      # expected: 0, GDP is complete
```

**What it shows:** still 270 rows, and every row found its GDP value (0 rows without a partner). The panel now has one more column, `gdp_pps_index`.

### 4.3.3 Education

```{r}
#| label: show-join-education
# 4.3.3 Add tertiary education
gap_panel <- gap_panel |>                                  # the panel so far
  left_join(education_wide,                                # add the education columns
            by = join_by(country_code, year))              # match on country and year

nrow(gap_panel)   # must still be 270

gap_panel |>
  anti_join(education_wide, by = join_by(country_code, year)) |>   # rows with no education data
  nrow()                                                           # expected: 0, education is complete
```

**What it shows:** still 270 rows, and every row found its education values (0 rows without a partner). The panel now has three more columns: `tertiary_women_pct`, `tertiary_men_pct` and `tertiary_gap`.

### 4.3.4 Deaths from all causes

```{r}
#| label: show-join-deaths
# 4.3.4 Add deaths from all causes
gap_panel <- gap_panel |>                                  # the panel so far
  left_join(deaths_all_causes,                             # add the deaths columns
            by = join_by(country_code, year))              # match on country and year

nrow(gap_panel)   # must still be 270

gap_panel |>
  anti_join(deaths_all_causes, by = join_by(country_code, year)) |>   # rows with no deaths data
  count(year)                                                         # expected: only 2024, 27 rows
```

**What it shows:** still 270 rows. The 27 rows without deaths data are exactly the 27 countries in 2024, the year the deaths table does not yet cover. In these rows the three death columns are `NA`. After the four joins, `gap_panel` has 270 rows and 15 columns, and its only missing values are these 27 rows of deaths and the two rows of healthy life years for Luxembourg.

## 4.4 Country names and the Baltic states

Two columns make the panel easier to read and to chart. `country` holds the English name of each country, because codes such as `EL` (Greece) or `SI` (Slovenia) are not known to every reader. `baltic` is `TRUE` for Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania and `FALSE` for the other 24 countries, so that every chart can highlight the three countries with one line of code.

The names are written once, in a small table with one row per country, and joined onto the panel by `country_code`, in the same way as the data tables.

```{r}
#| label: show-country-names
# 4.4 The English name of each EU member state, one row per country
country_names <- tibble(
  country_code = c("AT", "BE", "BG", "CY", "CZ", "DE", "DK", "EE", "EL",
                   "ES", "FI", "FR", "HR", "HU", "IE", "IT", "LT", "LU",
                   "LV", "MT", "NL", "PL", "PT", "RO", "SE", "SI", "SK"),
  country      = c("Austria", "Belgium", "Bulgaria", "Cyprus", "Czechia",        # same order as the codes above
                   "Germany", "Denmark", "Estonia", "Greece",
                   "Spain", "Finland", "France", "Croatia", "Hungary",
                   "Ireland", "Italy", "Lithuania", "Luxembourg",
                   "Latvia", "Malta", "Netherlands", "Poland", "Portugal",
                   "Romania", "Sweden", "Slovenia", "Slovakia")
)

nrow(country_names)   # should be 27
```

```{r}
#| label: show-baltic
# 4.4 Add the country names and mark the Baltic states
gap_panel <- gap_panel |>                                   # the panel after the four joins
  left_join(country_names, by = join_by(country_code)) |>   # add the name, matched on the code only
  mutate(baltic = country_code %in% c("EE", "LV", "LT")) |> # TRUE for Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania
  select(country_code, country, baltic, everything())       # put the three columns first, then all others

nrow(gap_panel)          # must still be 270
sum(is.na(gap_panel$country))   # expected: 0, every code found its name

gap_panel |>
  count(baltic) |>                                          # rows per group
  kable(col.names = c("Baltic state", "Rows"))              # expected: FALSE 240, TRUE 30
```

**What it shows:** still 270 rows, and every country code found its name (0 missing). 30 rows are marked as Baltic (3 countries times 10 years) and 240 as not Baltic. `gap_panel` now has 17 columns: code, name and Baltic mark first, then `year` and the 13 measures.

## 4.5 Saving the panel

The two combined tables are saved to `data/clean/`: `gap_panel.csv`, one row per country and year, and `deaths_by_cause.csv`, one row per country, year and cause, with the country names and the Baltic mark added so it can be charted on its own. `write_csv()` writes a table to a CSV file, and missing values are written as `NA`. The files in `data/clean/` are created by this code and can always be recreated by running the document again, unlike the files in `data/raw/`.

```{r}
#| label: show-save
# 4.5 Save the two combined tables to data/clean/
write_csv(gap_panel,                                        # the panel: one row per country and year
          here("data", "clean", "gap_panel.csv"))

deaths_by_cause <- deaths_by_cause |>                       # the deaths: one row per country, year and cause
  left_join(country_names, by = join_by(country_code)) |>   # add the names, as in the panel
  mutate(baltic = country_code %in% c("EE", "LV", "LT"))    # and the Baltic mark

write_csv(deaths_by_cause,
          here("data", "clean", "deaths_by_cause.csv"))
```

**Check: the saved panel loads again.** This is also the five-line check of the course checkpoint: load the clean data from its file and look at it, without any of the code above.

```{r}
#| label: show-checkpoint
# 4.5 Check: load the saved panel from the file, as anyone else would
here("data", "clean", "gap_panel.csv") |>    # the path to the saved file
  read_csv(show_col_types = FALSE) |>        # read it back
  glimpse() |>                               # show columns and types
  nrow()                                     # expected: 270
```

**What it shows:** the saved file loads with 270 rows and 17 columns, the same as `gap_panel` in memory. The types survived the round trip: `country_code` and `country` are text, `baltic` is logical (`TRUE` or `FALSE`), and all measures are numbers. `gap_panel.csv` is the table that Section 5 starts from.
